title: Phones away for the day
src:
Since 2023, all NSW public high schools have required students to keep their phones switched off and out of sight for the whole school day, including recess and lunch. The policy followed a similar move in primary schools and in several other states.

Supporters argue that the change has made classrooms calmer. Teachers report fewer interruptions and say students are talking to each other more at lunchtime. Some principals have also linked the ban to a fall in online bullying during school hours, although they acknowledge that problems can simply move to the evening.

Not everyone is convinced. Some parents want to be able to contact their children directly, especially when travelling to and from school. Researchers also point out that the evidence for improved academic results is mixed; studies from overseas show small gains in some schools and none in others. They suggest that how a ban is enforced matters more than the rule itself.

Schools can grant exemptions, for example for students who use phones to monitor medical conditions. Most schools store devices in lockers or pouches, while others simply trust students to keep phones in their bags. Teachers say consistency is the key: if staff apply the rule differently, students quickly test the limits.
points: NSW high schools ban phones all day since 2023
Benefits: calmer classes, more face-to-face talk, less bullying at school
Concerns: parents' contact, mixed evidence on results
Exemptions exist and consistent enforcement is key
qs: When must NSW high school students keep their phones away?
For the whole school day, including recess and lunch.
What do researchers say about the effect on academic results?
The evidence is mixed: small gains in some schools and none in others; enforcement matters more than the rule.
Why is consistency important?
If teachers apply the rule differently, students test the limits.

title: Why teenagers can't sleep
src:
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up late and are impossible to wake in the morning. Sleep scientists say this is not simply laziness. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts, so the hormone melatonin, which makes us feel sleepy, is released up to two hours later than in childhood.

At the same time, teenagers still need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night. With school starting early, many get far less. Surveys suggest that around 70 per cent of Australian high school students are not getting enough sleep on school nights.

The effects are significant. Lack of sleep is linked with poorer concentration, lower marks, irritability and a higher risk of anxiety and depression. Tired teenagers are also more likely to be involved in car accidents once they start driving.

Screens make the problem worse. Light from phones delays melatonin further, and social media can keep young people awake long after they planned to sleep. Experts recommend keeping devices out of bedrooms and maintaining a regular sleep schedule, even on weekends. Some schools overseas have trialled later start times, with promising results for attendance and mood, but changing timetables involves transport, sport and parents' work hours, which makes reform difficult.
points: Teen body clocks shift later; not laziness
Most teens get too little sleep
Effects on learning, mood, safety
Screens worsen it; tips and later school starts
qs: What biological change affects teenagers' sleep?
Their body clock shifts, so melatonin is released up to two hours later.
List two consequences of insufficient sleep.
Poor concentration, lower marks, irritability, anxiety/depression risk, car accidents (any two).
Why is changing school start times difficult?
It affects transport, sport and parents' work hours.

title: Small courses, big change
src:
A growing number of Australian workers are turning to microcredentials: short, focused courses that teach a specific skill, such as data analysis, project management or first aid. They may take a few weeks rather than several years, and many can be completed online in the evening.

Employers say microcredentials help staff keep up with fast-changing technology. Rather than returning to university for a full degree, an employee can learn exactly what a new role requires. Universities and TAFEs have responded by offering hundreds of such courses, and the federal government has funded a pilot program and created a national platform where learners can compare options.

However, there are concerns about quality and recognition. Because microcredentials are new, there is no single standard, and an employer in one industry may not know what a particular certificate is worth. Some experts worry that learners could spend money on courses that do not lead to better jobs. Others note that people who already have degrees are the most likely to enrol, which may increase rather than reduce inequality.

To address these issues, the government introduced a national framework that describes the length, level and assessment of each course. Supporters believe that, if quality is maintained, microcredentials could make lifelong learning a normal part of working life.
points: Microcredentials are short skill-focused courses
Employers value them for keeping up with change; institutions and government have expanded them
Concerns: quality, recognition, inequality
National framework introduced; could normalise lifelong learning
qs: What is a microcredential?
A short, focused course teaching a specific skill, often online, taking weeks not years.
Why might microcredentials increase inequality?
People who already have degrees are most likely to enrol.
What has the government done about quality concerns?
Introduced a national framework describing length, level and assessment.

title: Learning a language later in life
src:
It is often said that children learn languages more easily than adults. While young children do have an advantage in developing native-like pronunciation, researchers now believe adults have strengths of their own.

Adults can understand grammar rules more quickly, use strategies such as note-taking and spaced review, and connect new words to existing knowledge. Studies of adult migrants show that motivation and opportunities to use the language matter far more than age alone. People who work, volunteer or socialise in the new language usually progress faster than those who only attend classes.

Learning a language may also be good for the brain. Some studies have found that bilingual people tend to show symptoms of dementia several years later than monolingual people, although scientists continue to debate the reasons.

The biggest obstacles for adults are often practical: limited time, family responsibilities and fear of making mistakes in public. Teachers recommend setting small, regular goals and accepting errors as part of learning rather than a sign of failure.
points: Children have a pronunciation advantage, but adults have strengths
Adults use grammar understanding and strategies; motivation and use matter most
Possible brain benefits, e.g. delayed dementia
Obstacles are practical; set small goals and accept errors
qs: In what area do children have an advantage?
Developing native-like pronunciation.
What matters more than age for adult migrants?
Motivation and opportunities to use the language, such as work, volunteering or socialising.
What practical obstacles do adults face?
Limited time, family responsibilities and fear of making mistakes in public.

title: Robots in the warehouse
src:
Online shopping has transformed warehouses. To deliver orders faster, many large companies now use robots that move shelves, sort parcels and carry goods to human workers, who then pick and pack the items.

Companies say automation reduces physically demanding work and allows them to process orders more quickly and accurately. Some warehouse workers agree that robots have taken over the heaviest lifting and the long walks between shelves.

Others report that the pace of work has increased. When machines set the speed, workers may feel pressure to meet strict targets, with less time for breaks. Unions have raised concerns about injuries caused by repetitive movements, as well as constant monitoring through scanners and software.

Economists disagree about the long-term effect on jobs. Some predict that automation will reduce the number of warehouse positions, while others argue that new roles, such as robot maintenance and logistics planning, will replace them. Most agree that workers will need retraining, and that governments and employers share responsibility for providing it.
points: Online shopping has led to warehouse automation
Benefits: less heavy work, faster and more accurate
Concerns: pace, injuries, monitoring
Job effects debated; retraining needed
qs: How do robots work alongside humans in warehouses?
They move shelves, sort parcels and bring goods to human workers who pick and pack.
What concerns have unions raised?
Faster pace and strict targets, repetitive-movement injuries and constant monitoring.
On what do most economists agree?
Workers will need retraining, which governments and employers share responsibility for.

title: The value of school camps
src:
For generations, Australian students have packed sleeping bags for school camp. Activities range from bushwalking and canoeing to cooking meals in small groups. Although camps involve significant planning and cost, many teachers believe they offer learning that is difficult to achieve in the classroom.

Camps can build independence, as students manage their own belongings and routines away from home. Outdoor challenges encourage resilience and teamwork, and teachers often notice quieter students showing leadership in new settings. Relationships between staff and students also tend to improve after spending several days together.

Yet camps are not equally accessible. Fees can be a barrier for low-income families, and some students with disabilities or anxiety may find the experience overwhelming without proper support. Teachers also carry heavy responsibility for safety, often working long hours without extra pay.

Many schools now offer financial assistance and work with families before camp to plan for individual needs. Some have shifted to shorter or local programs to reduce cost while keeping the core benefits.
points: Camps are a long tradition offering learning beyond the classroom
Benefits: independence, resilience, teamwork, relationships
Barriers: cost, additional needs, teacher workload
Schools respond with assistance, planning, shorter local camps
qs: Name two benefits of school camps.
Independence, resilience, teamwork, leadership opportunities, better staff–student relationships (any two).
Why are camps not equally accessible?
Fees can be a barrier for low-income families; some students with disabilities or anxiety need support.
How have some schools reduced costs?
By offering shorter or local programs.

title: Coding in the primary classroom
src:
Since the introduction of the Digital Technologies curriculum, Australian primary students have been learning the basics of coding. Young children might program a small robot to follow a path, while older students create simple games using block-based languages.

Supporters argue that coding teaches far more than computer skills. Breaking a problem into steps, testing ideas and fixing errors develop logical thinking and persistence. Coding can also be creative and collaborative, especially when students design projects together.

However, many primary teachers report feeling underprepared. Most trained before digital technologies became part of the curriculum, and professional learning opportunities vary widely between schools. Access to devices and reliable internet is also uneven, particularly in some regional and remote areas.

Education researchers suggest that coding works best when linked to other subjects, such as using data in science or creating interactive stories in English. They also stress that teachers do not need to be experts; learning alongside students can model curiosity and problem solving.
points: Primary students learn coding through the curriculum
Develops logic, persistence, creativity
Teacher preparation and access are uneven
Integrate with other subjects; teachers can learn alongside students
qs: What skills do supporters say coding develops?
Logical thinking and persistence through breaking problems into steps, testing and fixing errors; creativity and collaboration.
Why do many primary teachers feel underprepared?
They trained before digital technologies were in the curriculum, and professional learning varies.
How do researchers suggest coding works best?
Linked to other subjects, such as science data or interactive stories in English.

title: Why we procrastinate
src:
Almost everyone puts off tasks they know they should do. Psychologists say procrastination is not simply laziness or poor time management. Instead, it is often a way of avoiding unpleasant emotions linked to a task, such as boredom, anxiety or fear of failure.

When we delay a task, we feel immediate relief. This short-term reward makes procrastination a habit that is hard to break, even though the stress usually returns, often stronger, as deadlines approach. Perfectionists are particularly prone, because starting a task means risking work that is less than ideal.

Research suggests several practical strategies. Breaking a large task into very small first steps reduces the emotional barrier to starting. Setting a timer for a short period, such as twenty-five minutes, can make work feel manageable. Removing distractions, especially phones, also helps.

Interestingly, studies have found that students who forgave themselves for procrastinating on one exam procrastinated less before the next. Self-criticism, it seems, can make the problem worse.
points: Procrastination is about avoiding emotions, not laziness
Short-term relief makes it a habit; perfectionists prone
Strategies: small steps, timers, removing distractions
Self-forgiveness reduces procrastination
qs: What is procrastination often a way of avoiding?
Unpleasant emotions linked to a task, like boredom, anxiety or fear of failure.
Why are perfectionists prone to procrastination?
Starting means risking work that is less than ideal.
What was surprising about self-forgiveness?
Students who forgave themselves procrastinated less next time; self-criticism makes it worse.

title: Drones on the farm
src:
Australian farmers are increasingly using drones to manage their properties. Fitted with cameras and sensors, drones can survey large paddocks in minutes, checking crop health, counting livestock and inspecting water troughs and fences that might otherwise take hours to reach by vehicle.

Some drones can also spray fertiliser or pesticide on specific parts of a field instead of covering the entire crop. This targeted approach can reduce chemical use and costs, and limits damage to surrounding environments.

The technology is not without problems. Good drones and the software to analyse their images can be expensive, and pilots require training and must follow aviation safety rules. In many rural areas, slow or unreliable internet makes it difficult to upload and process large amounts of data.

Despite these barriers, agricultural experts expect drone use to grow, especially as prices fall and as farmers face labour shortages. Some agricultural colleges now include drone operation in their courses.
points: Farmers use drones to survey and monitor
Targeted spraying reduces chemicals
Barriers: cost, training, rules, internet
Use expected to grow; colleges teach it
qs: List two tasks drones perform on farms.
Checking crop health, counting livestock, inspecting troughs and fences, targeted spraying (any two).
How can targeted spraying help?
It reduces chemical use and costs and limits environmental damage.
Why might internet access be a problem?
Slow or unreliable rural internet makes uploading and processing data hard.

title: Reading on screens
src:
More and more reading now happens on screens, from news articles to university textbooks. Researchers have compared how well people understand texts read on paper and on digital devices, and the results have surprised some educators.

Several large reviews have found that, for longer informational texts, readers tend to understand slightly more when reading on paper, particularly when under time pressure. One explanation is that people skim more on screens, a habit developed through scrolling social media and websites. Readers also tend to overestimate how well they have understood digital texts.

For short texts or stories, the difference is small or absent. And digital texts offer real advantages, including adjustable font sizes, built-in dictionaries and easy searching, which can particularly help students with reading difficulties.

Researchers suggest that the medium matters less than how we read. Slowing down, taking notes and checking understanding can reduce the screen disadvantage. Teachers are encouraged to explicitly teach students strategies for deep reading on digital devices.
points: Research compares paper and screen comprehension
Paper slightly better for long texts; skimming and overconfidence on screens
Small difference for short texts; digital advantages
How we read matters most; teach deep reading strategies
qs: For which texts is paper reading slightly better?
Longer informational texts, especially under time pressure.
What explanation is given for weaker screen comprehension?
People skim more on screens and overestimate their understanding.
What advantages do digital texts offer?
Adjustable fonts, built-in dictionaries and searching, helping students with reading difficulties.

title: Teacher shortages
src:
Schools across Australia are struggling to find enough teachers, especially in mathematics, science and regional areas. Principals report combining classes, using teachers outside their specialist area, and cancelling elective subjects.

Several factors contribute. Fewer students are choosing teaching degrees, and a significant number of early-career teachers leave within their first five years. Surveys of teachers point to heavy workloads, administrative tasks and challenging student behaviour as the main reasons people consider leaving.

Governments have responded in a number of ways. These include scholarships for teaching students, higher salaries in some states, paid placements, and fast-track programs for career changers. There are also efforts to reduce paperwork so teachers can focus on teaching.

Education experts say that pay matters, but it is not the whole answer. Strong mentoring for new teachers, manageable timetables and respect for the profession are just as important. Without them, they warn, schools will continue to train teachers only to lose them a few years later.
points: Teacher shortages, esp. maths, science, regional
Causes: fewer entrants, early-career teachers leaving due to workload
Government responses: scholarships, pay, placements, fast-track
Experts: mentoring, timetables, respect matter as much as pay
qs: Which subjects and areas are most affected?
Mathematics, science and regional areas.
Why do many teachers consider leaving?
Heavy workloads, administrative tasks and challenging student behaviour.
Besides pay, what do experts say is important?
Mentoring for new teachers, manageable timetables and respect for the profession.

title: Wearable health trackers
src:
Smartwatches and fitness bands now track steps, heart rate, sleep and even blood oxygen levels. Millions of Australians wear them daily, and many say the devices motivate them to move more.

Research suggests wearables can modestly increase physical activity, especially when people set goals and receive regular feedback. Some devices have detected irregular heart rhythms, prompting users to seek medical help in time.

However, the accuracy of measurements varies, particularly for sleep and calories burned. Some users become anxious about their data or feel guilty when they miss targets. Doctors also report patients arriving with worries based on readings that turn out to be unimportant.

Privacy is another concern. Health data collected by wearables may be stored overseas or shared with other companies, and users rarely read the terms. Experts recommend checking privacy settings and treating the numbers as a general guide rather than a medical diagnosis.
points: Wearables are widely used and motivate activity
Benefits include heart rhythm detection
Accuracy issues and anxiety
Privacy concerns; use as a guide
qs: What benefits of wearables are mentioned?
Modest increases in activity with goals and feedback; detecting irregular heart rhythms.
What are the accuracy concerns?
Measurements vary, especially for sleep and calories.
What do experts recommend?
Check privacy settings and treat numbers as a guide, not a diagnosis.

title: Bilingual schooling
src:
In some Australian primary schools, students learn half their subjects in English and half in another language, such as Mandarin, Indonesian or Spanish. These bilingual programs aim to develop strong skills in both languages from an early age.

Research generally shows that students in good bilingual programs perform as well as, or better than, their peers in English literacy over time, even though they spend less time learning in English. They also develop high levels of proficiency in the second language and tend to show greater flexibility in thinking.

Programs can be particularly valuable for children whose families speak the second language at home, as they maintain and strengthen their heritage language rather than losing it.

The main challenge is staffing. Bilingual programs need teachers who are both qualified and highly proficient in the target language, and such teachers are scarce. Programs also require long-term commitment, since the benefits appear over several years rather than immediately.
points: Bilingual programs teach subjects in two languages
Students match or exceed peers and gain flexibility
Supports heritage languages
Staffing and long-term commitment are challenges
qs: How do bilingual students perform in English literacy?
As well as or better than peers over time, despite less time learning in English.
Why are programs valuable for heritage-language families?
Children maintain and strengthen their heritage language rather than losing it.
What is the main challenge?
Finding qualified teachers who are highly proficient in the target language.

title: Apprenticeships making a comeback
src:
For many years, school leavers were encouraged to go to university, and trade apprenticeships were sometimes seen as a second choice. That attitude is changing. Skills shortages in areas such as electrical work, plumbing and construction mean qualified tradespeople are in high demand, and many earn well.

Apprenticeships allow people to earn while they learn, combining paid work with training at TAFE or a private provider. Apprentices finish without the student debt that many university graduates carry. Government incentives for employers and fee-free TAFE places have also encouraged more people to start.

However, completion rates remain a concern, as many apprentices do not finish their training. Reasons include low wages in the early years, difficult workplace relationships and a lack of support. Women remain under-represented in most trades.

Industry groups say better mentoring, higher first-year wages and safer, more inclusive workplaces would help more apprentices complete their qualifications.
points: Attitudes to trades changing; skills shortages
Earn while learning, no debt, incentives, fee-free TAFE
Low completion; women under-represented
Solutions: mentoring, higher wages, inclusive workplaces
qs: Why are tradespeople in high demand?
Skills shortages in areas like electrical work, plumbing and construction.
What financial advantage do apprenticeships have?
Earning while learning and finishing without student debt.
Why do many apprentices not finish?
Low early wages, difficult workplace relationships, lack of support.

title: Paying with phones
src:
Cash is rapidly disappearing from Australian life. Most payments are now made by card, phone or smartwatch, and the share of transactions made in cash has fallen sharply over the past decade. Some cafés and shops no longer accept cash at all.

Digital payments are fast and convenient, and they make it easier for people to track their spending. Businesses save time on counting and banking cash, and the risk of theft is reduced.

However, some groups rely on cash, including older people, people in remote areas with unreliable connectivity and those who use cash to manage tight budgets. Natural disasters and network outages also show the risk of depending entirely on electronic systems. In addition, card surcharges can make small purchases more expensive.

Consumer advocates have called for laws to guarantee access to cash for essential goods and services. The federal government has indicated it will require certain businesses to accept cash for essentials, aiming to balance innovation with fairness.
points: Cash use has fallen sharply
Digital is convenient for customers and businesses
Some groups need cash; outages and surcharges
Calls to guarantee cash for essentials
qs: Why do businesses prefer digital payments?
They save time counting and banking cash and reduce theft risk.
Which groups rely on cash?
Older people, people in remote areas, and those managing tight budgets.
What have consumer advocates called for?
Laws guaranteeing access to cash for essential goods and services.

title: Mental health days for students
src:
Some education systems overseas now allow students to take a small number of mental health days each year, counted as legitimate absences. The idea has prompted debate in Australia.

Supporters say such days acknowledge that mental health is as important as physical health. They argue that allowing a day of rest can prevent problems from building up, and that it encourages young people to talk openly about how they feel.

Critics worry that students might use the days to avoid tests or difficult situations, and that avoidance can make anxiety worse over time. Some teachers also note that missing school can create extra stress when students fall behind.

Many psychologists suggest that mental health days could be useful if they are part of a broader approach. This would include access to school counsellors, teaching students coping skills and following up with students who frequently need time away. A day off, they argue, should be the start of a conversation rather than a replacement for support.
points: Some overseas systems allow mental health days; debated here
Supporters: equal importance, prevention, openness
Critics: avoidance and falling behind
Psychologists: part of broader support
qs: What do supporters say mental health days acknowledge?
That mental health is as important as physical health.
Why are critics concerned?
Students may avoid tests or difficult situations, and avoidance can worsen anxiety; missing school creates stress.
What broader approach do psychologists recommend?
Counsellor access, teaching coping skills and following up with students who often need time away.

title: Remote learning lessons
src:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, millions of Australian students learned from home for weeks or months at a time. The experience provided an unplanned experiment in remote education.

Some students thrived. They enjoyed working at their own pace, avoided distractions in the classroom and developed independence. Teachers rapidly improved their digital skills, and many schools continue to use online platforms for homework and communication.

Others struggled. Students without reliable internet, a quiet place to work or parents available to help fell further behind. Younger children and students with disabilities found remote learning particularly difficult, and many young people reported feeling isolated from friends.

Researchers concluded that schools are about much more than delivering content. Relationships with teachers and peers, structure, and support services all play vital roles. The main lesson, many argue, is that technology should support face-to-face teaching rather than replace it.
points: Pandemic created a remote learning experiment
Some thrived; teachers gained digital skills
Others struggled due to access, age, disability, isolation
Schools are about relationships; tech should support teaching
qs: Which students thrived in remote learning?
Those who enjoyed working at their own pace and developed independence.
Which students struggled most?
Those without internet, quiet space or parental help; younger children; students with disabilities.
What is the main lesson, according to many?
Technology should support face-to-face teaching rather than replace it.

title: Public libraries reinvented
src:
Public libraries were once mainly places to borrow books in silence. Today, many Australian libraries look very different. Alongside books, they offer free internet, maker spaces with 3D printers, homework clubs, English conversation classes and even tool and seed libraries.

Librarians say these changes reflect what communities need. For people without a computer at home, libraries are essential for applying for jobs, accessing government services and completing schoolwork. For new migrants, they are often among the first welcoming public spaces they encounter. On hot days, air-conditioned libraries also provide a free place to escape the heat.

The shift has brought challenges. Libraries must balance quiet study areas with noisier activities, and staff now need skills in technology and community programs as well as information services. Funding from councils has not always kept pace with these expanding roles.

Despite this, visitor numbers at many modern libraries remain strong. Advocates argue that libraries are one of the few public places where anyone can spend time without being expected to buy something.
points: Libraries now offer much more than books
They meet community needs: digital access, migrants, heat refuge
Challenges: noise balance, staff skills, funding
Visits remain strong; free public space
qs: What new services do libraries offer?
Free internet, maker spaces with 3D printers, homework clubs, English conversation classes, tool and seed libraries.
Why are libraries important for people without home computers?
For applying for jobs, accessing government services and doing schoolwork.
What challenges have the changes created?
Balancing quiet and noisy spaces, new staff skills, and funding not keeping pace.

title: Maths anxiety
src:
Maths anxiety is a feeling of tension or fear that interferes with a person's ability to work with numbers. It is surprisingly common: international surveys suggest that around a third of 15-year-olds feel very tense when doing maths homework, and many adults avoid tasks involving numbers.

Researchers have found that anxiety uses up working memory, the mental space needed to hold information while solving a problem. As a result, anxious students may perform poorly even when they understand the content. Over time, avoidance can lead to real gaps in skills, which then increase anxiety further.

The causes are varied. Timed tests, public questioning and messages that maths ability is fixed can all contribute. Adults also play a role: studies have found that children of parents who are anxious about maths sometimes learn less during the year, particularly when those parents help frequently with homework.

Teachers can reduce maths anxiety by emphasising effort and strategies rather than speed, normalising mistakes and giving students opportunities to succeed before tasks become harder. Short writing activities, in which students describe their worries before a test, have also been shown to improve performance for some students.
points: Maths anxiety is common and interferes with maths
It uses working memory and leads to avoidance and gaps
Causes include timed tests, fixed-ability messages, anxious parents
Teachers can reduce it through effort focus, normalising mistakes, early success
qs: Why can anxious students perform poorly even if they understand the content?
Anxiety uses up working memory needed to solve problems.
How can parents unintentionally contribute to maths anxiety?
Anxious parents who help frequently with homework may pass on anxiety, and children may learn less.
Name two strategies teachers can use.
Emphasise effort/strategies over speed, normalise mistakes, give early success, short writing before tests (any two).

title: Explicit instruction
src:
Explicit instruction is a teaching approach in which the teacher clearly explains a new skill, models it step by step and then guides students through practice before they work independently. It is sometimes summarised as "I do, we do, you do".

Supporters point to cognitive load theory, which suggests that working memory is very limited when learning new information. When beginners are asked to discover a method entirely on their own, they can become overloaded and learn little. Clear explanations and worked examples reduce unnecessary load, allowing students to focus on the key ideas.

In mathematics, explicit instruction is often used for new procedures, such as solving equations. Teachers check understanding frequently, using techniques such as mini whiteboards, and provide immediate feedback. As students become more skilled, the support is gradually removed.

Critics argue that too much teacher talk can make students passive and that problem solving and curiosity may be neglected. Many educators now see the two approaches as complementary: explicit teaching to build foundations, followed by richer problems in which students apply and extend what they have learned.
points: Explicit instruction: explain, model, guide, then independent practice
Supported by cognitive load theory
Used for maths procedures with frequent checks and feedback
Critics: passive students; most see approaches as complementary
qs: What does 'I do, we do, you do' mean?
Teacher models, then guided practice together, then independent practice.
How does cognitive load theory support explicit instruction?
Working memory is limited; discovery can overload beginners; explanations and worked examples reduce load.
What view do many educators now hold?
The approaches are complementary: explicit teaching for foundations, then richer problems.

title: Data science in schools
src:
As data becomes central to almost every industry, some educators argue that schools should teach data science alongside traditional mathematics. Data science combines statistics, programming and subject knowledge to find patterns and answer questions using large data sets.

Advocates say that many students find calculus abstract but are motivated by questions about sport, health or the environment that can be explored with real data. Free tools such as spreadsheets and Python notebooks make it possible to analyse thousands of records in a classroom.

Several countries have introduced data science courses for senior students, and in Australia, data skills appear in both the mathematics and digital technologies curriculums. However, few schools offer a dedicated course, partly because teachers need training in both statistics and programming.

Critics warn that data science should not replace the algebra and calculus needed for engineering and science degrees. They suggest instead that data investigations be built into existing subjects. Either way, there is broad agreement that students must learn to question data: where it came from, who collected it and whether conclusions are justified.
points: Calls to teach data science in schools
Advocates: motivating real questions, free tools
Few dedicated courses; teacher training needed
Critics: keep algebra/calculus; all agree students must question data
qs: What does data science combine?
Statistics, programming and subject knowledge.
Why do advocates think data science motivates students?
Questions about sport, health or the environment with real data are more engaging than abstract calculus.
What do critics suggest instead?
Build data investigations into existing subjects rather than replace algebra and calculus.

title: Calculators: friend or foe?
src:
Few classroom tools have caused as much debate as the calculator. Since the 1970s, teachers, parents and researchers have argued about when and how students should use them.

Research reviews have generally found that calculator use does not harm students' basic skills when it is combined with regular teaching of mental strategies. In some studies, students who used calculators developed better attitudes towards mathematics and were more willing to tackle complex problems.

However, many teachers report that some students reach for a calculator for very simple calculations, such as 7 × 8, and cannot estimate whether an answer is reasonable. Without number sense, a student may accept an obviously wrong answer caused by a keying error.

For this reason, most curriculums now distinguish between non-calculator and calculator tasks. Students are expected to develop fluency with mental and written methods, while also learning to use calculators and software efficiently for complex or realistic problems. The key question, teachers say, is not whether to use calculators, but when they genuinely support learning.
points: Calculators long debated
Research: no harm with mental strategy teaching; better attitudes
Concern: over-reliance and lack of number sense
Curriculums use both; key is when calculators support learning
qs: What have research reviews generally found?
Calculators don't harm basic skills if combined with teaching of mental strategies; may improve attitudes.
Why is number sense important when using a calculator?
Students need to estimate and notice when a keying error gives an obviously wrong answer.
How do most curriculums handle calculators now?
They separate non-calculator and calculator tasks.

title: AI and academic integrity
src:
The arrival of powerful AI chatbots has forced schools to rethink assessment. A tool that can write an essay, solve an equation or produce working code in seconds makes it difficult to know whether take-home work reflects a student's own ability.

Some schools initially banned AI tools, but many have since moved towards guided use. Students may use AI to brainstorm or check understanding, provided they acknowledge it, while key assessments are completed under supervision or include an oral component in which students explain their work.

Detection software has proved unreliable. Studies have found that it can wrongly flag genuine work, particularly writing by students learning English, which raises serious fairness concerns.

Many educators argue that the most effective response is to design assessments that value process as well as product. In computing, for example, students might submit planning documents, testing logs and a short video explaining their code. Such tasks are harder to complete with AI alone and give teachers a clearer picture of students' thinking.
points: AI chatbots challenge assessment
Shift from bans to guided, acknowledged use and supervised tasks
Detection software unreliable and unfair
Design tasks that value process
qs: Why has AI made take-home assessment difficult?
AI can produce essays, solutions and code instantly, so work may not reflect the student's ability.
What is the problem with AI detection software?
It's unreliable and can wrongly flag genuine work, especially by English learners.
What kind of assessment do educators recommend?
Tasks valuing process and product: planning, testing logs, explanations.

title: Girls in computing
src:
Although girls perform as well as boys in mathematics and digital technologies in Australian schools, far fewer choose senior computing subjects or technology degrees. Women make up only around a quarter of Australia's technology workforce.

Research suggests that the gap is driven less by ability than by confidence and identity. Many girls do not see themselves as "computer people", often because of stereotypes in media and a lack of visible role models. Experiences in junior classes also matter: girls are more likely to lose interest when tasks seem disconnected from real-world problems.

Schools that have increased female participation often use several strategies together. These include inviting women working in technology to speak to students, framing projects around social impact, such as apps that support the community, and creating clubs where beginners feel welcome.

Industry groups argue that improving diversity is not only a matter of fairness. Teams with a range of backgrounds are more likely to notice problems and design technology that works well for everyone.
points: Girls perform equally but few choose computing
Gap due to confidence, identity, stereotypes
Strategies: role models, social impact, welcoming clubs
Diversity improves technology
qs: What does research suggest drives the gender gap?
Confidence and identity, stereotypes and lack of role models, not ability.
Name two strategies schools have used.
Women speakers, social-impact projects, welcoming beginner clubs (any two).
Why does industry say diversity matters beyond fairness?
Diverse teams notice problems and design technology that works for everyone.

title: The cost of cyber attacks on schools
src:
Schools and universities have become frequent targets for cyber criminals. They store valuable personal information, including students' medical details and family contacts, yet often have limited budgets for security.

One of the most common attacks is phishing, in which staff receive an email that appears to come from a trusted source and are tricked into revealing their passwords. Another is ransomware, which locks an organisation's files until a payment is made. In some overseas cases, schools have been forced to close for days.

Experts recommend a layered approach. Multi-factor authentication means that a stolen password alone is not enough to access an account. Regular software updates close known security gaps, and backups stored separately from the main network allow data to be restored after an attack.

Perhaps most important is training. Because many attacks rely on human error, staff and students who can recognise suspicious messages provide a crucial line of defence. Several education departments now require annual cybersecurity training for all employees.
points: Schools targeted: valuable data, small budgets
Phishing and ransomware are common
Layered defence: MFA, updates, separate backups
Training most important; departments require it
qs: Why are schools attractive targets?
They hold valuable personal information but have limited security budgets.
What is ransomware?
Malware that locks files until a payment is made.
Why is training considered so important?
Many attacks rely on human error, so people who recognise suspicious messages are a key defence.

title: Mini whiteboards
src:
Few classroom tools are as simple, or as powerful, as the mini whiteboard. When a teacher asks a question, every student writes an answer and holds it up at the same moment. In a few seconds, the teacher can see who has understood and who needs help.

This technique addresses a common problem with traditional questioning. When teachers ask a question and choose a volunteer, they usually hear from the most confident students, while others stay silent. Whole-class responses give every student a reason to think and allow teachers to gather evidence from the entire group.

In mathematics, mini whiteboards are particularly useful for checking procedures, such as simplifying expressions, because errors are immediately visible. Teachers can then decide whether to move on, reteach a step or work with a small group.

To be effective, routines matter. Teachers recommend practising the procedure, using a clear signal for students to show their boards, and keeping questions short. Used well, mini whiteboards turn a lesson into a continuous conversation about learning.
points: Every student answers at once; teacher sees understanding
Fixes volunteer-only questioning
Useful for spotting maths errors and deciding next steps
Needs clear routines
qs: What problem with traditional questioning do mini whiteboards solve?
Volunteers are usually confident students; others stay silent. Whole-class responses involve everyone.
Why are they especially useful in maths?
Errors in procedures are immediately visible.
What routines make them effective?
Practise the procedure, clear signal to show, short questions.

title: Spaced practice in maths
src:
Many students prepare for maths tests by completing dozens of questions on a single topic just before the exam. This feels productive, but research suggests that it is not the best way to remember skills over time.

Spaced practice involves revisiting topics repeatedly over weeks or months. Because some forgetting occurs between sessions, students must work harder to recall the method, which strengthens long-term memory. Interleaving, which mixes different types of problems, adds another benefit: students must decide which strategy to use, just as they will in an exam.

In one well-known study, students who practised mixed problems scored significantly higher on a delayed test than those who practised one type at a time, even though their practice scores were lower.

Teachers can build spacing into everyday lessons by starting with a short review of earlier topics and setting homework that includes questions from previous units. Explaining the research to students is also helpful, as many interpret difficulty as a sign of failure rather than a sign that learning is happening.
points: Cramming feels productive but is less effective
Spacing strengthens memory through effortful recall
Interleaving improves delayed test results
Teachers: daily review, mixed homework, explain research
qs: Why is cramming one topic not the best approach?
It feels productive but doesn't support long-term memory.
What is interleaving and why does it help?
Mixing problem types; students must choose the strategy, as in exams.
How can teachers build spacing into lessons?
Start with review of earlier topics; homework including previous units.

title: Financial literacy in maths
src:
With rising living costs and easy access to credit, many educators believe that young Australians need stronger financial skills before they leave school. Financial literacy includes understanding budgets, interest, superannuation, tax and the true cost of borrowing.

Much of this content already appears in the mathematics curriculum, through topics such as percentages, rates and compound interest. However, teachers say that students often learn the calculations without connecting them to real decisions, such as choosing a phone plan or understanding "buy now, pay later" services.

Surveys of young adults show that many feel unprepared to manage money, and some find themselves in debt soon after leaving school. Programs that use realistic scenarios, such as planning a budget for a first apartment, appear to improve both skills and confidence.

Some commentators want financial literacy to become a separate compulsory subject. Others argue that it is better integrated into mathematics, where students can see how calculations support everyday decisions.
points: Young people need financial skills
Content exists in maths but lacks real connections
Many feel unprepared; realistic scenarios help
Debate: separate subject or integrated
qs: What does financial literacy include?
Budgets, interest, superannuation, tax and the cost of borrowing.
What problem do teachers notice with current teaching?
Students learn calculations without linking them to real decisions.
What two views about delivery are mentioned?
A separate compulsory subject vs integrating into mathematics.

title: Learning to program: why errors help
src:
For many beginners, the first experience of programming is a screen full of red error messages. Students who expect to write perfect code often become frustrated and conclude that they are "not good at coding".

Experienced programmers see errors differently. Debugging, the process of finding and fixing mistakes, is a normal and constant part of software development. Professional developers often spend more time testing and debugging than writing new code.

Teachers can help students adopt this mindset. Some ask students to predict what a program will do before running it, then investigate any difference between the prediction and the result. Others use "bug hunts", where students fix deliberately broken programs, making errors a game rather than a failure.

Research on novice programmers suggests that clear, beginner-friendly error messages and structured debugging strategies, such as testing small parts of a program at a time, significantly reduce frustration. Over time, students learn that persistence and systematic thinking matter more than getting everything right the first time.
points: Beginners frustrated by errors
Debugging is normal for professionals
Strategies: predict and run, bug hunts
Clear messages and systematic debugging reduce frustration
qs: Why do many beginners become frustrated?
They expect perfect code and see error messages as failure.
How do professionals view debugging?
As a normal, constant part of development; they spend much time on it.
Describe one teaching strategy mentioned.
Predict-then-run, bug hunts with broken programs, testing small parts (any one).

title: Mathematics and Aboriginal knowledge
src:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures contain rich mathematical knowledge, from patterns in weaving and art to navigation using the stars and the seasonal calendars used to manage land. Australian curriculums now encourage teachers to include these perspectives in mathematics lessons.

Advocates say this can increase engagement for Aboriginal students, who may see their culture reflected in the classroom, and can help all students appreciate that mathematics exists in every culture, not only in textbooks.

Examples include investigating symmetry and transformations in traditional designs, using kinship systems to explore logic and patterns, or studying how fish traps were engineered to work with tides.

However, educators stress that this work must be done respectfully. Teachers should consult local Aboriginal communities and education consultants, avoid treating cultures as all the same, and recognise that some knowledge is not meant to be shared publicly. When done well, partnerships with local Elders can enrich learning for the whole school.
points: Aboriginal cultures contain rich maths knowledge
Benefits for engagement and understanding
Classroom examples: symmetry, logic, fish traps
Must be respectful and community-led
qs: Give two examples of mathematical knowledge in Aboriginal cultures.
Patterns in weaving/art, star navigation, seasonal calendars, fish traps, kinship systems (any two).
What benefits do advocates mention?
Increased engagement for Aboriginal students; all students see maths in every culture.
What must teachers do to approach this respectfully?
Consult local communities, avoid generalising, respect knowledge not meant to be shared.

title: Flipped classrooms
src:
In a flipped classroom, students watch short instructional videos or read material at home, and class time is used for practice, problem solving and discussion. The idea is to move the passive part of learning out of the classroom so that teachers can support students when they apply new skills.

In mathematics, flipped learning allows students to pause and replay explanations as many times as they need. In class, the teacher can circulate, identify misconceptions and work closely with small groups.

However, the model depends on students completing the preparation. If many students arrive without watching the video, lessons can quickly fall apart. Students without reliable internet access at home may also be disadvantaged.

Research on flipped classrooms has produced mixed results. Benefits appear strongest when videos are short, include questions that students must answer, and when teachers check preparation at the start of each lesson. Many teachers now use a partial flip, introducing some topics in class and flipping others.
points: Flipped: content at home, practice in class
Benefits for maths: replay, teacher support in class
Risks: unprepared students, internet access
Mixed research; short videos with checks; partial flip
qs: What happens in a flipped classroom?
Students learn content at home through videos/reading; class time is for practice and discussion.
What are two risks of the model?
Students not preparing; students without internet disadvantaged.
When are the benefits strongest?
Short videos with questions, and teachers checking preparation at the start of lessons.

title: Student data privacy
src:
Schools collect large amounts of information about students, from attendance and results to health conditions and photographs. Increasingly, this information is stored on cloud platforms and shared with educational apps.

Privacy experts warn that some apps collect more data than necessary, including location or browsing behaviour, and may share it with third parties for advertising. Children are particularly vulnerable because they rarely understand what they are agreeing to.

Australian privacy law requires organisations to handle personal information responsibly, and education departments have guidelines on approving digital tools. However, teachers often sign up for free apps without checking how data is used, simply because they want to try something new in class.

Experts recommend that schools maintain a list of approved tools, read privacy policies before adopting new apps and collect only the data they genuinely need. Teaching students about privacy is equally important, so that they can make informed decisions about their own information online.
points: Schools collect and store lots of student data, often in the cloud
Some apps over-collect and share data
Laws and guidelines exist but teachers sign up without checks
Approved lists, read policies, minimise data, teach privacy
qs: What kinds of student data do schools collect?
Attendance, results, health conditions, photographs.
Why are children particularly vulnerable?
They rarely understand what they are agreeing to.
What do experts recommend schools do?
Keep an approved tools list, read privacy policies, collect only necessary data, teach students about privacy.

title: Project-based learning in computing
src:
Project-based learning (PBL) asks students to investigate a real problem over an extended period and produce a product for a real audience. In computing subjects, this might mean designing a website for a local charity or building a database for the school library.

Supporters argue that PBL mirrors how technology is developed in industry. Students must research users' needs, plan, build a prototype, test it and improve it. Along the way, they develop teamwork, communication and project management skills that are difficult to teach through short exercises.

However, PBL can be difficult to manage. Projects may take longer than planned, some group members may contribute little, and students can spend too much time on appearance rather than functionality. Weaker students may struggle without clear structure.

Effective teachers address these issues by breaking projects into milestones, teaching key skills explicitly before students need them, assigning clear team roles and assessing both the final product and each student's individual contribution.
points: PBL: extended real problems with real audiences
Mirrors industry and builds soft skills
Challenges: time, unequal contribution, weaker students
Solutions: milestones, explicit teaching, roles, individual assessment
qs: What is project-based learning?
Students investigate a real problem over time and produce a product for a real audience.
Why do supporters say PBL suits computing?
It mirrors industry development: research users, plan, prototype, test, improve.
How do effective teachers manage PBL?
Milestones, explicit teaching of skills, clear roles, assess individual contribution.

title: NAPLAN online
src:
Since moving online, Australia's NAPLAN tests in literacy and numeracy use a format called adaptive testing. As students answer questions, the test adjusts its difficulty: students who perform well receive more challenging questions, while others receive questions closer to their level.

Supporters say this gives more precise information about each student's achievement, particularly for students at the high and low ends, who previously answered many questions that were too easy or too hard. Results are also returned to schools more quickly than with paper tests.

The move online has brought challenges. In the early years, some schools experienced technical problems, and teachers raised concerns that students with limited typing skills or device experience might be disadvantaged.

Teachers can help students prepare by ensuring that they are familiar with the online format, including tools such as on-screen calculators and rulers. Many educators emphasise that NAPLAN is a snapshot of learning on one day, best used alongside classroom assessment rather than as the sole measure of a student's progress.
points: Online NAPLAN uses adaptive testing
More precise and faster results
Challenges: technical issues, typing/device skills
Prepare students; use as one snapshot
qs: What is adaptive testing?
The test adjusts difficulty based on the student's answers.
What are two advantages of online NAPLAN?
More precise information, especially at high/low ends; faster results.
How should NAPLAN results be used, according to educators?
As a snapshot alongside classroom assessment, not the only measure.

title: Mathematics in the workplace
src:
Employers across many industries report that new workers often lack confidence with everyday mathematics. Surveys of Australian businesses have found that problems with percentages, measurement and interpreting data are common, even among school leavers with good results.

The mathematics used at work is often different from that taught in school. Rather than solving neatly presented problems, workers must decide which information matters, estimate quickly and check whether results make sense. A nurse calculating a medication dose or a builder estimating materials cannot afford a careless error.

Some educators argue that school mathematics should include more contextual problems that resemble workplace tasks. Vocational education programs often do this well, embedding numeracy in practical tasks such as costing a job or reading technical drawings.

Others caution against reducing mathematics to only practical skills. Abstract reasoning, they say, prepares students for jobs that do not yet exist. Most agree, however, that students benefit from seeing how mathematics is used in real careers.
points: Employers report weak everyday maths
Workplace maths requires judgement, estimation and checking
Calls for contextual problems, as in vocational programs
Abstract reasoning still important; real careers help
qs: What maths problems do employers commonly report?
Difficulties with percentages, measurement and interpreting data.
How is workplace maths different from school maths?
Workers must select relevant information, estimate and check results, rather than solve neat problems.
Why do some caution against only practical maths?
Abstract reasoning prepares students for future jobs that don't yet exist.

title: Gamification in learning
src:
Gamification means adding game elements, such as points, badges and leaderboards, to activities that are not games. Many educational apps now use these features to encourage students to practise skills such as times tables or vocabulary.

Research suggests that gamification can increase participation, especially for routine practice. Immediate feedback and visible progress give students a sense of achievement.

However, there are risks. Leaderboards may motivate high achievers while discouraging students who are always near the bottom. Some students focus on collecting points rather than understanding, for example by guessing quickly. When the rewards are removed, motivation may fall.

Educators suggest using gamification carefully: rewarding effort and improvement rather than only correct answers, allowing students to compete against their own previous scores, and ensuring that games support clear learning goals. Game-based learning, where students play or design games that require mathematical thinking, may offer deeper benefits than simply adding points.
points: Gamification adds game elements to learning
Increases participation in routine practice
Risks: leaderboards, guessing, reliance on rewards
Use carefully; game-based learning may be deeper
qs: What is gamification?
Adding game elements like points, badges and leaderboards to non-game activities.
What are two risks?
Leaderboards discourage lower achievers; focus on points not understanding; motivation drops when rewards removed (any two).
How should educators use gamification?
Reward effort/improvement, compete against own scores, link to clear learning goals.

title: Teaching statistics with real data
src:
Traditional statistics lessons often use small, invented data sets with tidy numbers. While these are convenient, they rarely reflect the messy data that people encounter in real life.

A growing number of teachers now use real data from sources such as the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the Bureau of Meteorology or sports organisations. Students might investigate whether summers are getting hotter, compare the heights of basketball and netball players, or analyse survey data collected from their own class.

Working with real data raises valuable questions. Students must decide what to do with missing values, consider whether a sample is representative and think about how data collection might introduce bias. These are exactly the skills needed to evaluate claims in the media.

The main challenges are time and technology. Large data sets require spreadsheets or statistical software, and students need guidance to avoid being overwhelmed. Teachers recommend starting with a clear question and a manageable subset of data before expanding the investigation.
points: Invented data rarely reflects reality
Teachers use real sources and class data
Real data raises questions of missing values, samples, bias
Challenges: time and tech; start small
qs: What is the problem with traditional statistics data?
Small invented data sets with tidy numbers that don't reflect real, messy data.
Name two sources of real data.
ABS, Bureau of Meteorology, sports organisations, class surveys (any two).
What do teachers recommend to avoid overwhelming students?
Start with a clear question and a manageable subset of data.

title: Early career teachers
src:
The first years of teaching are often described as both rewarding and overwhelming. New teachers must plan lessons, manage classes, assess students and communicate with families, frequently while still learning the routines of their school.

Australian studies suggest that a significant proportion of early career teachers consider leaving the profession within their first five years. Common reasons include heavy workload, behaviour management challenges and feeling isolated.

Schools that retain new teachers tend to provide structured support. This includes a reduced teaching load in the first year, a trained mentor who meets regularly with the new teacher, and opportunities to observe experienced colleagues. Access to shared, high-quality lesson resources also saves considerable planning time.

New teachers themselves can protect their wellbeing by setting realistic boundaries, asking for help early and focusing on a small number of priorities, such as clear routines and positive relationships. Experienced teachers often remind beginners that confidence comes with time.
points: Early years are rewarding but overwhelming
Many consider leaving: workload, behaviour, isolation
Schools retain teachers with structured support
Teachers protect wellbeing with boundaries and priorities
qs: Why do many early career teachers consider leaving?
Heavy workload, behaviour challenges and feeling isolated.
What support do successful schools provide?
Reduced load, trained mentor, observing colleagues, shared resources.
What can new teachers do themselves?
Set boundaries, ask for help early, focus on a few priorities.

title: Cloud computing in schools
src:
Many Australian schools have moved their documents, email and learning platforms to the cloud, meaning that data is stored on remote servers managed by large technology companies rather than on computers at the school.

The benefits are considerable. Students and teachers can access their work from any device with an internet connection, files are backed up automatically, and collaboration becomes easier because several people can edit the same document at once. Schools also save money on maintaining their own servers.

However, cloud computing depends on a reliable internet connection. When the network fails, learning can stop. Questions also arise about where data is stored, who can access it and what happens if a provider changes its terms or suffers a security breach.

IT experts advise schools to choose providers that store data securely, ideally in Australia, to train staff and students in good security practices and to keep offline alternatives available for essential tasks such as examinations.
points: Schools moving to the cloud
Benefits: access, backups, collaboration, savings
Risks: internet reliance, data location and security
Advice: secure providers, training, offline backups
qs: What does it mean to store data in the cloud?
Data is kept on remote servers managed by technology companies, not at the school.
Give two benefits of cloud computing for schools.
Access from any device, automatic backup, easier collaboration, lower costs (any two).
What advice do IT experts give?
Choose secure providers (ideally Australian storage), train users, keep offline alternatives.

title: Coding to learn mathematics
src:
Programming and mathematics have always been closely linked, but some teachers now use coding as a way to teach mathematical ideas directly. Instead of only solving equations on paper, students write short programs that generate patterns, simulate probability experiments or draw geometric shapes.

Supporters say that coding makes abstract ideas concrete. A student who writes a loop to add up the first hundred numbers gains a feel for sequences and series. Simulating thousands of coin tosses in seconds shows how experimental probability approaches theoretical probability far more convincingly than a handful of real tosses.

There are practical challenges. Many mathematics teachers have little programming experience, and time spent learning syntax can take away from mathematical content. Some students also become focused on getting the code to work rather than on the mathematics behind it.

Teachers who use this approach successfully tend to provide partly completed programs that students modify, rather than asking them to write everything from scratch. Collaboration between mathematics and computing teachers also helps.

It makes abstract ideas concrete (series, probability)
Challenges: teacher skills, syntax time, focus on code
Use partly completed programs; collaborate

Writing a loop to sum numbers builds a feel for series; simulating coin tosses shows experimental probability approaching theoretical.
What challenges are mentioned?
Teachers lack programming experience; syntax takes time from maths; students focus on code not maths.
How do successful teachers use this approach?
Give partly completed programs to modify; collaborate with computing teachers.

title: Meditation apps helping children affected by trauma
src:
Schools in the Northern Territory are turning to an unusual tool to manage difficult behaviour: meditation apps. Teachers hope the apps will reduce disruption in classrooms and give children who have experienced trauma hope for a better future.

The need is clear. So far this year, public schools in the Territory have gone into lockdown 16 times because of student behaviour. Last year the figure was even higher, with 31 lockdowns recorded.

At St Joseph's Catholic College in Katherine, staff are trialling an app called Smiling Mind, which was developed by psychologists. Teachers use it at moments when students are most unsettled, such as straight after lunch, recess or other busy activities. A few minutes of guided breathing and quiet reflection help the class settle before learning begins.

Staff say that teaching mindfulness and emotional regulation helps students to calm their bodies and manage their feelings. This is particularly valuable for children with complex needs, because the app gives them practical strategies to control strong emotions and stay calm when they feel overwhelmed.

Dr Addie Wootten, who leads the organisation behind Smiling Mind, says that teachers and families are increasingly asking for more support in this area.

Smiling Mind is not the only app being tested. Schools in the ACT, New South Wales and New Zealand are trialling a different app created by the Australian Childhood Trauma Group. Each morning, students use it to record how they are feeling, how well they slept and whether they have eaten.

The aim is to check whether each student is ready to learn that day and, if not, to identify what is getting in the way. The app produces reports for school welfare teams, so staff can talk with a student early, before a problem develops, or contact parents when necessary.

Gregory Nicolau, from the Australian Childhood Trauma Group, believes schools need to change the way they respond to challenging behaviour. In his view, schools should stop blaming and shaming children and move away from old methods that do not work. When teachers understand how students are feeling and whether they are ready to learn, he argues, disruptive behaviour can be prevented before it even starts.

title: Help for parents struggling with back-to-school costs
src:
For many families, the start of the school year arrives at the worst possible time. Straight after the expense of Christmas and New Year, parents must pay for new uniforms, shoes, hats, books and stationery.

Courtney Jarvis is one parent feeling the pressure. She says the cost of basic items such as school shirts, shorts and hats is difficult to manage so soon after the holidays. Her situation is harder because her son Silvester, who is starting preschool, has muscular dystrophy, a condition that brings significant extra costs.

In North Queensland, help is available through School Savvy, a program run by Centacare NQ. It allows parents to buy uniforms and school supplies at low prices. Last year the program assisted 2,500 families, and this year it is expanding to the Burdekin, Mount Isa and Cloncurry regions.

Centacare says demand for discounted school supplies has grown this year because the high cost of living is putting real pressure on households. Parent Maria Tracey is one of those who benefited. The program saved her a couple of hundred dollars, which she says makes a big difference when everyday prices keep rising.

Another response has come from the community itself. In 2020, Alison Schutt and her husband Jan started a charity called Stationery Aid. The idea came from their own home: their children kept bringing back exercise books and stationery that had hardly been used, yet no organisation would accept them as donations.

Stationery Aid now collects used exercise books and stationery and gives them a second life. Volunteers remove the used pages and students' names, then repair or cover the books so they look new before passing them on to students in need.

The couple considered sending the items overseas, but decided to focus on Australian students because the need in their own community is so great. Stationery Aid estimates that about one per cent of Queensland students need some help to start the school year with the basic equipment they require.

Local sewing groups also contribute, making fabric pencil cases and library bags so that students receive a complete set of supplies.

title: Students restoring their school forest
src:
On the outskirts of Bundaberg, about 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, Gooburrum Primary School has something most schools can only dream of: its own forest. The pine forest is around 70 years old and covers two hectares of the school grounds.

For students, the forest is an outdoor classroom and a playground at the same time. They play there, have lessons, explore, and carry out science activities among the trees. Children watch the clouds and the birds, search for lizards and insects, dig holes and play in the mud.

A few years ago, however, drought killed about 400 of the trees. The loss upset many students and staff, who had grown attached to the forest.

Rather than accept the damage, the school community decided to bring the forest back. Students now play the central role in its regeneration, planting and caring for hundreds of new trees. Each student's tree carries a small copper tag with their name on it, and every year students are photographed beside their tree so they can see how much both the tree and they themselves have grown.

The replanting has also changed the character of the forest. Instead of replacing the pines, the school chose native species. These trees attract birds and small insects and provide bush food, and the school believes they will help local plants and animals and make the forest stronger and healthier in the long term.

Year 6 student Sebastian Walz and teacher Mechalle Kimber both describe the forest as a calm and relaxing place that helps students feel happier. Ms Kimber adds that not every child learns well in an ordinary classroom, and the forest gives them another place where they can succeed.

Gardening presenter Costa Georgiadis agrees that nature has therapeutic benefits. He explains that looking at fractals, the repeating patterns found in leaves and branches, is deeply calming, rather like listening to classical music, and helps people feel relaxed and at home.

When students finish Year 6, the school marks the moment in a special way. Photos showing each child and their tree growing over the years are displayed, and the whole school forms a guard of honour to farewell them.

title: Students send bacteria into space to brew yoghurt
src:
A group of Australian high school students is sending bacteria into space, with an unusual goal: to find out whether yoghurt can be made in orbit.

Forty students from schools across Victoria are taking part in the program, working in partnership with Swinburne University of Technology. Among them is a team from Haileybury, an independent high school in Melbourne.

The yoghurt cultures will travel to the International Space Station on board a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, launching from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The launch is scheduled for 5:06am US time on Tuesday, which is just after 9pm in Australia.

The experiment has two main aims. The first is to see how low gravity affects bacteria. The second is more practical: to work out the best way for astronauts to make their own yoghurt during long missions, when fresh food is hard to supply.

In total, 36 small vials will be sent to the space station. Each vial contains frozen milk together with the "good" bacteria used to make yoghurt. Two types of milk are being tested: full cream cow's milk and soy milk.

Once on board, the samples will be allowed to ferment for different lengths of time: 24, 48 or 72 hours. They will then be frozen again for the journey home, which is expected to take about a month and a half before the samples arrive back in Australia.

When the yoghurts return, the students will compare them with samples made on Earth. They will analyse how thick each yoghurt is, how healthy it is, and how much lactic acid it contains.

For the students involved, the project is a rare chance to design a real scientific experiment and see it carried out in space.

title: Queensland's longest school bus run
src:
When Jazane George wakes up in his home on an outback Indigenous reserve each morning he yawns, stretches and listens to the sounds of the river that runs past the doorstep of his home.

But he can't stand around enjoying it for too long.

He is up earlier than most for his commute to school, which takes more than an hour, depending on whether there's wildlife to contend with, on Queensland's longest school bus run.

Despite the distance, the 10-year-old is keen as mustard to get out the door when he hears the school bus arrive.

"I only saw a bull on the way in today," he laughs.

The bus whisks its way along 120 kilometres of sealed road, a rarity among the vast red outback plains.

Jazane is one of 18 students who board the bus each day from the Bidunggu Aboriginal Reserve in the remote Gulf of Carpentaria.

Covering 240 kilometres a day, Burketown State School students have already had a long day before they even enter the classroom.

The Indigenous community is home to around 60 residents perched nearby the Gregory River, more than 300km from the nearest city, Mount Isa.

Burketown principal Chris Ford said the school was approached by elders from Bidunggu to get the program up and running four years ago.

"The community had tried to run remote education through school of the air but there was limited technology, and trying to teach paper resources with unreliable mail services just wasn't working," he said.

"In education the big focus is that every student should never be left behind, so having a community that wants kids getting to school was a really good opportunity to help."

A driver and supervisor travel 120km to collect the students each morning before journeying back to school.

In the afternoon, the process is repeated in reverse with the bus racking up just under 500km per school day.

"Now we have up to 18 students coming a day, they make up a bit less than 50 per cent of the school population," Mr Ford said.

The bus is funded by the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR), but the Waanyi native title holders support the roster of teaching staff and parents who help keep the wheels turning.

By the end of the school year, students will have travelled nearly 50,000km — more than four times the average car registered in Queensland.

It's a huge difference compared to the average student in south-east Queensland, who will travel less than 8km per day to get to school, a figure that hasn't changed much in the past three decades.

But being on the road doesn't seem to bother these kids.
