title: Wellbeing dogs help students manage anxiety
src:
When a group of Year 5 students at St Monica's Primary School in Canberra suggested introducing a wellbeing dog last year, the school principal, Lisa Harris, was very supportive of the idea.

The students had researched how a wellbeing dog could reduce anxiety and improve learning outcomes. The principal agreed because she had noticed the effects of COVID-19 on children. Many students were experiencing higher levels of anxiety, feeling worried about attending school and displaying behavioural problems.

After researching the benefits of having a wellbeing and support dog, the school staff began looking for a suitable dog. Fortunately, a Year 2 teacher, June Edwards, was already considering getting another family pet when she heard about the school's discussion. She immediately volunteered to help.

Monty, a cavoodle, was adopted by the Edwards family when he was just eight weeks old. He became part of the school community from the very beginning and even attended a staff meeting on the day he arrived.

Before interacting with students, Monty received his full vaccinations and completed a training course. Teachers and students were also taught how to interact with him safely and appropriately.

Initially, Monty spent several months at the school full-time. He now visits the school part-time, but teachers say his calming presence has made a significant difference to students' behaviour and emotional wellbeing.

One of the most noticeable improvements has been in students experiencing school refusal. Unlike truancy, which generally involves deliberately staying away from school, school refusal is a stress response that makes attending school extremely difficult for a young person.

Before Monty arrived, many students would enter the school office but refuse to go into their classrooms. However, teachers have noticed that some of these students are now much more willing to attend school because they look forward to seeing Monty.

One teacher also described the experience of a young boy who had difficulty separating from his mother in the morning. Previously, he struggled to enter the school independently. However, with Monty's support, he gradually became comfortable walking along the corridor and entering his classroom.

Research has shown that therapy animals can have several positive effects on students. These include improving their mood, learning engagement, communication skills and confidence. They can also reduce emotional distress associated with attending school.

Students at St Monica's have shared positive experiences since Monty became part of their school community.

One Year 4 student explained that school life had become better and that Monty had encouraged her to participate in more activities.

Another student, who previously had a fear of dogs, gradually became comfortable around them because of her interactions with Monty. She eventually overcame her fear and even got a cavoodle of her own.

Similar benefits have been reported by educational institutions across Australia. These include primary schools in Cobar and Young in New South Wales, a kindergarten in Tasmania and the University of Western Australia.

title: How memory really works
src:
Good morning. Today I want to talk about something every student cares about, which is how to remember what you study. Let's start with a common habit. Many students prepare for exams by rereading their notes and highlighting key sentences. It feels productive. The text looks familiar, and familiarity gives us a sense that we know the material. Unfortunately, research consistently shows that rereading is one of the least effective study methods. Recognising information is not the same as being able to recall it.

So what works better? The first strategy is called retrieval practice. Instead of looking at the information again, you try to bring it back from memory. This could mean answering practice questions, using flashcards, or simply closing your book and writing down everything you can remember about a topic. In one well-known experiment, students who read a passage once and then tested themselves remembered around fifty per cent more a week later than students who read it several times. The effort of retrieving is exactly what strengthens the memory.

The second strategy is spacing. When we cram, we pack all our study into one long session just before the exam. Cramming can work for the next day, but the information fades quickly. If, instead, you spread your study over several shorter sessions, separated by days, you remember much more over the long term. A useful rule of thumb is to review new material the next day, then a few days later, then a week later.

The third strategy is interleaving, which means mixing different types of problems rather than practising one type at a time. In mathematics, for example, students often complete twenty questions on the same skill. Interleaving mixes questions from different topics. It feels harder, and students usually believe they are learning less. But because they must decide which method to use each time, their performance in tests is often significantly better.

Now, you might be wondering why so many people still rely on rereading and cramming. The answer is that effective learning often feels difficult, while ineffective learning feels easy. Researchers call these desirable difficulties. My advice is to trust the evidence rather than your feelings. If studying feels slightly uncomfortable, that may be a sign that it is working.

For next week, I'd like you to try one of these strategies in another subject and keep a short record of what you did. We'll compare notes in the tutorial.

title: The science of habits
src:
Welcome back to the show. Today I want to talk about habits, and why some are so easy to form while others seem impossible. Researchers estimate that a large part of what we do each day is habitual. We don't consciously decide to brush our teeth or check our phones; we simply do it.

A habit is usually described as a loop with three parts. First, there's a cue, something that triggers the behaviour, like waking up or feeling bored. Second, there's the routine, which is the behaviour itself. And third, there's a reward, the good feeling that makes the brain want to repeat it. Checking your phone, for example, can be triggered by boredom and rewarded by a small hit of novelty.

So how long does it take to form a new habit? You may have heard twenty-one days. In fact, one well-known study from University College London found it took participants an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become automatic, with a huge range from about eighteen days to over two hundred, depending on the person and the habit. Simple habits, like drinking a glass of water at breakfast, formed faster than complex ones, like doing fifty sit-ups before dinner.

The good news is that missing a day didn't seriously damage progress. What mattered was consistency over time.

So what does this mean in practice? Experts suggest three strategies. Start very small. If you want to exercise, begin with five minutes, not an hour. Link the new habit to an existing one, a technique called habit stacking. For instance, after I pour my morning coffee, I'll write one sentence in my journal. And change your environment. If you want to eat more fruit, put it on the bench; if you want to use your phone less, leave it in another room.

Breaking bad habits works in reverse. Make the cue harder to notice and the behaviour harder to do. Willpower, it turns out, is far less reliable than design.
points: Much daily behaviour is habitual

title: Changing the school day
src:
Speaker A: Today we're discussing whether the school day should change. With me is education researcher Professor Leanne Moore. Leanne, most Australian schools run from about nine until three. Where did that come from?
Speaker B: Largely from history. The timetable developed when many families had one parent at home and children were needed for chores. Society has changed a great deal, but the school day mostly hasn't.
Speaker A: Some people argue high schools should start later. Why?
Speaker B: Sleep research shows that teenagers' body clocks shift, so they naturally fall asleep and wake later. When schools start early, many students are chronically tired. Studies from the United States found that when some high schools moved their start time to around eight-thirty or later, attendance improved, students reported better mood, and there were fewer car accidents involving teenage drivers.
Speaker A: So why don't all schools do it?
Speaker B: Practical reasons. Later starts affect bus timetables, which are often shared with primary schools. They push after-school sport and part-time jobs later. And many parents rely on schools for childcare while they work.
Speaker A: Are there other ideas for changing the day?
Speaker B: Yes. Some schools are trialling flexible timetables, where senior students attend fewer days on campus and study independently on others. Others offer extended hours with optional before- and after-school programs, which helps working parents. In some countries, schools have longer breaks in the middle of the day.
Speaker A: What's your view?
Speaker B: I don't think there's one perfect model. But I'd like to see more schools trial later starts for older students and measure the results carefully. Decisions should be based on evidence and on consultation with students, families and teachers, rather than on habit.
Speaker A: Professor Moore, thank you.

Teen body clocks support later starts; US evidence
Barriers: buses, sport, jobs, childcare
Alternatives: flexible timetables, extended hours, longer breaks
Recommend trials based on evidence and consultation

title: Managing exam stress
src:
Hi everyone. With the HSC only a few months away, I want to talk about stress, because nearly everyone in this room will feel some.

First, a little stress is actually useful. It increases focus and motivation; it's what gets you to open the textbook. Problems begin when stress becomes constant and overwhelming. Signs include trouble sleeping, headaches, irritability, feeling unable to concentrate, or withdrawing from friends. If you notice these, it's time to act.

So what helps? Let me give you four things. Number one: plan, don't panic. Break your revision into specific tasks, like complete two past papers for chemistry, rather than vague goals like study chemistry. Use a calendar and work backwards from your exam dates. A plan reduces the feeling that everything needs to be done at once.

Number two: protect your sleep. It's tempting to stay up late, but memory is consolidated while you sleep. Pulling an all-nighter before an exam usually lowers your performance.

Number three: keep moving and keep connected. Even a twenty-minute walk reduces stress hormones. Don't drop your sport or your part-time job completely, and spend time with friends. Balance is not a distraction from study; it makes study possible.

Number four: watch your self-talk. Thoughts like I'm going to fail everything or my life is over if I don't get my ATAR are common, but they're not facts. Try replacing them with something more realistic, like I've prepared for this and I'll do my best. Remember too that there are many pathways to university and careers, including bridging courses, TAFE and early entry programs.

Finally, ask for help. Your teachers, year adviser and school counsellor are here for you. Services like Kids Helpline and headspace are available too.

You've got this. And whatever happens, your results don't define your worth.

Plan specific revision tasks
Protect sleep; avoid all-nighters
Exercise, connection, balance; realistic self-talk
Many pathways; ask for help

title: Citizen science
src:
Thank you for coming to tonight's talk. I'd like to start with a question: how many of you have ever counted birds in your backyard, photographed a frog, or reported a whale sighting? If you have, you may already be a citizen scientist.

Citizen science means members of the public taking part in real scientific research, usually by collecting or analysing data. It isn't new; amateur naturalists have contributed to science for centuries. But smartphones and the internet have transformed what's possible. Today, one person's photo, uploaded to an app with a time and location, can become part of a data set used by researchers around the world.

Let me give you some Australian examples. The FrogID project asks people to record frog calls on their phones. Each species has a distinctive call, so experts can identify which frogs are present. Volunteers have submitted hundreds of thousands of recordings, helping scientists track how frogs responded to bushfires and drought, and even contributing to the discovery of species in new locations.

The Aussie Bird Count runs every October and involves people counting birds for twenty minutes. And projects like Redmap ask fishers and divers to report marine species seen outside their usual range, which helps scientists understand how warming oceans are shifting where species live.

Why does this matter? Professional scientists simply can't be everywhere. Citizen scientists provide data across huge areas and long periods of time, at very low cost. Participants also benefit. Research shows they gain scientific knowledge, feel more connected to nature and often become advocates for conservation.

Of course, there are challenges. Data quality can vary, so projects use expert checking and verification tools. Most participants also come from cities and from groups with higher education, so researchers are working to include more diverse communities, including Aboriginal rangers who bring deep knowledge of Country.

So tonight, I encourage you to download one of these apps and become part of the research.
points: Citizen science: public helping research, transformed by phones
Examples: FrogID, Aussie Bird Count, Redmap
Benefits for science and participants
Challenges: data quality, diversity; include Aboriginal rangers
Invitation to join

Members of the public taking part in real research, usually collecting or analysing data.

title: Learning from failure
src:
Good morning, everyone. I'd like to begin with a confession. In my first year of teaching, I planned what I thought was a brilliant lesson on probability, with dice, cards and a class competition. Within ten minutes, the room was chaos, two students were arguing, and nobody had learned anything about probability. I went home convinced I had chosen the wrong career.

I tell this story because we rarely talk honestly about failure in education, even though it's one of the most powerful sources of learning, for teachers and for students.

Research on what's often called productive failure supports this. In a series of studies, students who first attempted challenging problems on their own, and mostly failed, before receiving instruction, later showed deeper understanding than students who were taught the method first. The struggle seemed to prepare their minds to make sense of the explanation. The key word, though, is productive. The problems must be within reach, students must feel safe to make mistakes, and the teacher must then help them connect their attempts to the correct ideas.

That sense of safety matters enormously. If students believe mistakes will be punished or mocked, they'll avoid challenges altogether. So how do we create a classroom where failure is acceptable? A few practical ideas. Talk about your own mistakes, as I just have. When a student gets something wrong, ask them to explain their thinking before correcting them; often the error reveals a reasonable idea. Give feedback that focuses on the next step rather than just a mark. And, where possible, allow students to revise and resubmit work.

The same applies to us as teachers. That disastrous probability lesson taught me to give clearer instructions, set roles in group work and test activities before using them. The second time I taught it, it worked well.

So my challenge for today is this: in your groups, share one lesson that didn't go as planned, and what you learned from it. Let's model the culture we want our students to experience.

title: Cognitive load theory for teachers
src:
Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to introduce cognitive load theory, which has become one of the most influential ideas in education research and is now referred to in many teacher training programs.

The theory is based on a simple observation about human memory. Our working memory, the part of the mind that holds information while we think, is very limited. Most adults can hold only a few new pieces of information at once. Long-term memory, on the other hand, is almost unlimited. Learning, in this view, is the process of building organised knowledge in long-term memory, sometimes called schemas.

Why does this matter for teachers? When students face too much new information at once, their working memory becomes overloaded, and very little is learned. This is particularly true for novices. An expert mathematician can solve a complex equation easily because many steps are automatic, stored in long-term memory. A Year 8 student must consciously process every step.

So what can we do? First, break complex material into smaller steps and teach them in a logical sequence. Second, use worked examples. Research shows that for beginners, studying a fully worked example is often more effective than solving the same problem independently. Then we can gradually remove steps, a technique called fading. Third, reduce unnecessary distractions. If a slide has an explanation in text and the teacher is also explaining it aloud, students may waste effort trying to read and listen at the same time. Diagrams should be placed next to the relevant text, not on a different page.

An important point is that as students become more expert, the support should change. Worked examples that help beginners can actually become less useful for advanced students, who benefit more from solving problems themselves. This is known as the expertise reversal effect.

For your planning this week, I'd like you to take one lesson and identify where students might be overloaded, then redesign it using worked examples and fading. We'll share these at our next meeting.

Working memory limited; learning builds schemas in long-term memory
Novices overloaded more easily than experts

Expertise reversal; planning task for staff

Speaker A: Has that made a difference?

Speaker A: What should schools prioritise?
Speaker B: Three things. First, teacher training, because quality teaching is the biggest factor. Second, equity. Students in regional areas and low-income communities often have less access to devices and specialist teachers. And third, ethics. Students should think about the impact of the technology they create, from privacy to bias.

title: Making maths lessons engaging
src:
Good morning, everyone. I'd like to talk about something every maths teacher struggles with at some point: engagement. How do we make students genuinely want to think about mathematics?

Let me start with a common misunderstanding. Engagement is not the same as entertainment. A lesson full of games and videos can be fun but produce very little learning. Real engagement happens when students are thinking hard about the mathematics itself.

So how do we achieve that? The first strategy is to start with a question rather than an answer. Instead of saying, "Today we're learning about the area of a circle," try showing a large pizza and a small pizza with their prices and asking, "Which is better value?" Students immediately want to know, and they need the mathematics to find out.

The second strategy is to use what's called low floor, high ceiling tasks. These are problems that every student can start, but that can be extended a long way. For example, "How many squares are there on a chessboard?" Every student can count the small squares, but the full answer requires systematic thinking, and the most able students can generalise to any size board.

Third, make students' thinking visible. Ask them to explain, compare strategies and critique each other's reasoning. When a student says, "I did it a different way," that's a golden moment for discussion.

Finally, success matters. Students who constantly fail switch off, so make sure tasks are challenging but achievable, and give students regular evidence of their progress. A short review quiz at the start of each lesson, where most students do well, can build confidence and remind them how much they've learned.

None of these strategies requires expensive resources. They require careful planning and a belief that every student can think mathematically. I'll now share some examples from my own classroom.

Ensure success; review quizzes; no expensive resources needed

title: Digital wellbeing and young people
src:
Thank you for joining us tonight. My topic is digital wellbeing: how the technology young people use every day affects their health, relationships and learning.

First, some context. Most Australian teenagers now own a smartphone, and many spend several hours a day on screens outside school. Not all of this time is harmful. Teenagers use technology to stay in touch with friends, learn new skills and express their creativity. In fact, research suggests that moderate use is not associated with poorer wellbeing.

The concerns arise with heavy use, particularly late at night. Studies consistently link phone use in bed with shorter and poorer quality sleep, and lack of sleep affects mood, concentration and learning. Social media can also increase anxiety for some young people, especially when they compare themselves with idealised images or experience online conflict.

What can schools do? Many schools now restrict phone use during the day, and early reports suggest calmer classrooms and more face-to-face interaction. But restrictions alone are not enough. Students need to learn skills: how to manage notifications, recognise when an app is designed to keep them scrolling, protect their privacy and respond to online conflict. These skills can be taught in subjects like computing and personal development.

Parents also play a crucial role. One of the simplest and most effective steps is to keep devices out of bedrooms overnight, ideally charging them in a shared space. Parents can also model healthy habits, as children notice when adults are constantly on their phones.

Finally, it's important to involve young people in these conversations. When students help create family or school technology agreements, they are much more likely to follow them. Digital wellbeing is not about fear of technology; it's about helping young people use it in ways that support their lives rather than control them.

Concerns: night use harms sleep; social media anxiety
Schools: phone restrictions plus teaching skills

Involve young people; support not fear

title: Teaching probability with simulations
src:
Good morning. Today we're focusing on probability, a topic that students often find counter-intuitive. Even adults make predictable errors. For example, many people believe that after five heads in a row, tails is now "due". This is known as the gambler's fallacy, and it shows how our intuition about chance can mislead us.

One of the most effective ways to build understanding is through simulation. Let's take a simple experiment: rolling two dice and adding the numbers. If you ask Year 9 students which total is most likely, many will guess that every total is equally likely. If they roll the dice twenty times, the results are too few to show a clear pattern. But if they use a spreadsheet or a short program to simulate ten thousand rolls, the pattern appears immediately: seven is the most common total, and two and twelve are the least.

This leads naturally to the idea of theoretical probability. Students can list all thirty-six possible outcomes in a table and discover that there are six ways to make seven, but only one way to make two. The simulation and the theory confirm each other, which is very powerful.

Simulations are also useful for introducing the law of large numbers: as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability gets closer to the theoretical probability. Students can see this happen by graphing results after ten, one hundred and ten thousand trials.

A practical tip: don't start with the technology. Let students roll real dice first and make predictions. When their small sample gives surprising results, they will want to know what happens with more trials, and that's the moment to introduce the simulation.

Finally, connect probability to real contexts, such as weather forecasts, sports statistics or games of chance. Discussing why casinos always make money over time can be a very memorable way to explore expected value with senior students.

Simulating thousands of dice rolls reveals patterns
Links to theoretical probability (36 outcomes)
Law of large numbers shown by graphing trials
Start with real dice; use real contexts like casinos

title: Behaviour management for new teachers
src:
Hello, everyone. Behaviour management is consistently the area that beginning teachers worry about most, so let's look at what the research and experienced teachers say actually works.

The most important idea is that good behaviour is mostly built through prevention, not reaction. Teachers who rarely have serious problems are usually those who have taught clear routines from the first day. Students know exactly how to enter the room, how to start work, how to get help and how to pack up. When routines are clear, there are fewer opportunities for disruption.

Second, relationships matter. Learning students' names quickly, greeting them at the door and showing interest in their lives builds trust. Students are much more likely to cooperate with a teacher who they believe respects them.

Third, when problems occur, respond calmly and consistently. Use the least intrusive response first. Often a look, moving closer to the student or a quiet word is enough. Avoid public arguments, because students may feel they need to save face in front of their peers. If behaviour continues, follow the school's procedures and apply consequences consistently, so that students see the rules are fair.

Fourth, well-planned lessons prevent many problems. When work is too easy or too hard, students disengage. Having the first task ready as students enter and keeping transitions short reduces downtime, which is when most misbehaviour happens.

Finally, don't try to manage everything alone. Talk to your mentor, your head teacher and the year adviser. Experienced colleagues often know the students' backgrounds and can suggest strategies that work for particular individuals. Asking for help is a sign of professionalism, not weakness.

Remember that every experienced teacher had difficult lessons when they started. Reflect, adjust and keep going. Confidence will come.

Relationships build trust
Calm, least intrusive, consistent responses
Planned lessons and short transitions
Ask colleagues for help; confidence comes

title: Ethics in software development
src:
Good afternoon. In today's lecture on software engineering, we're stepping away from code to discuss something just as important: ethics.

Software now makes decisions that affect people's lives. Algorithms help decide who gets a loan, which job applicants are interviewed and what news people see. When these systems are poorly designed, the consequences can be serious.

Let's consider three key issues. The first is bias. If a system is trained on historical data that reflects past discrimination, it may repeat that discrimination. For example, a recruitment tool trained on data from a company that mostly hired men might rank female applicants lower, even if no one intended this. Developers must test their systems for unfair outcomes across different groups.

The second issue is privacy. Many apps collect far more personal data than they need. The principle of data minimisation says that we should collect only what is necessary for the purpose. Developers should also consider how data is stored, who can access it and how long it is kept.

The third issue is accessibility. Software that cannot be used by people with disabilities excludes a significant part of the population. Simple practices, such as providing text descriptions for images, ensuring sufficient colour contrast and supporting keyboard navigation, make a big difference.

Why should we teach these ideas to school students? Because they are the developers of the future. When students build even a small app, we can ask them: Who might be excluded? What data do we really need? Could this be misused? These questions encourage them to see technology as something that serves people, not just something that works.

For next week, I'd like you to analyse a popular app and identify one ethical issue related to bias, privacy or accessibility, with a recommendation for improvement.

title: Supporting students' mental health in senior years

Speaker A: What role do teachers play?
Speaker B: A huge one. Teachers see students every day, so they often notice changes before anyone else. A student who suddenly stops handing in work or seems withdrawn may be struggling. Speaker A: Should teachers try to solve the problem themselves?
Speaker B: No. Teachers aren't counsellors, and they shouldn't try to be. Their role is to notice, listen and refer students to the wellbeing team. Every school has procedures for this, and teachers should follow them, especially if there's any concern about a student's safety.
Speaker A: What about teaching practices?
Speaker B: Clear assessment schedules help a lot, so students aren't hit with several tasks in the same week. Teachers can also teach study skills, like breaking revision into small steps. And it's important that we talk about pathways. Students need to hear that there are many routes to university and careers, including alternative entry schemes and TAFE.
Speaker A: Any advice for parents?
Speaker B: Keep communication open, encourage balance, like exercise, sleep and time with friends, and avoid adding pressure about marks. Remind them that you're proud of their effort.

title: Assessment for learning in mathematics
src:
Good morning, colleagues. I want to talk about assessment, but not the kind that ends with a mark in a report. I'm talking about assessment for learning: the everyday practices that tell us, during a lesson, what students understand and what we should do next.

Research over several decades has shown that formative assessment, when done well, is one of the most powerful ways to improve student achievement. The key idea is simple. Teaching is only effective if we know whether students have learned what we intended. If we wait until the end-of-topic test, it's often too late to help.

So what does good formative assessment look like in a maths classroom? First, clear learning intentions. Students should know what they are learning and what success looks like. For example, "I can solve two-step equations and check my answer by substitution."

Second, frequent checks for understanding. Mini whiteboards, hinge questions and exit tickets allow us to gather evidence from every student, not just the confident volunteers. A well-designed hinge question has wrong answers that reveal specific misconceptions. If many students choose the same wrong answer, we know exactly what to reteach.

Third, feedback that moves learning forward. A mark alone tells a student very little. Comments such as "Check the sign when you move a term across the equals sign" are far more useful. Even better, give students time in class to act on the feedback.

Finally, involve students in assessing their own work and each other's. When students mark worked solutions against clear criteria, they begin to understand what quality looks like and become more independent learners.

None of this requires more marking. In fact, it often requires less, because we focus our effort where it makes a difference. I'd encourage each of you to choose one strategy to try in your classes this term.
points: Assessment for learning happens during lessons
Clear learning intentions and success criteria
Frequent checks: whiteboards, hinge questions, exit tickets
Specific feedback with time to act
Student self/peer assessment; less marking; try one strategy

Everyday practices during lessons that show what students understand and what to do next.

title: The induction gap
src:
When graduates begin their first teaching job, many are given the same timetable, duties and responsibilities as colleagues with twenty years of experience. Researchers call this the 'induction gap': the difference between what new teachers are expected to do and the support they actually receive.

In some schools, induction consists of a single morning of presentations about policies and procedures, after which new staff are left to manage on their own. Not surprisingly, surveys show that many beginning teachers feel overwhelmed by planning, marking and behaviour management in their first term.

By contrast, schools with strong induction programs provide a reduced teaching load, a trained mentor from the same subject area and regular opportunities to observe experienced colleagues. They also introduce new teachers gradually to extra responsibilities such as playground duty and report writing.

The benefits appear to be significant. New teachers in well-designed programs report greater confidence and job satisfaction, and they are more likely to remain in the profession beyond five years. Some education departments now fund release time for both mentors and new teachers, recognising that good induction is an investment rather than a cost.

title: Timetables that work
src:
Few people outside schools realise how complex it is to build a school timetable. In a typical secondary school, a timetabler must schedule more than a thousand students, eighty teachers, dozens of specialist rooms and hundreds of elective combinations, all within a fixed number of periods each week.

Modern timetabling software can test millions of possible arrangements, but human judgement is still essential. For example, software may produce a timetable that is technically valid but places a class's three mathematics lessons on the same afternoon, or gives a new teacher five consecutive periods with difficult classes.

Good timetablers therefore combine the software's speed with knowledge of their school. They try to spread core subjects across the week, avoid scheduling practical subjects immediately after lunch when rooms need cleaning, and give beginning teachers a manageable load. Many also consult faculty heads before finalising the timetable.

When timetabling works well, nobody notices. When it fails, the effects can be felt for a whole year: frustrated students, exhausted teachers and wasted resources.

title: Advice for first-year teachers
src:
Good afternoon, and congratulations on your first teaching positions. I've been in schools for twenty-six years, and I want to share three pieces of advice that I wish someone had given me.

First, don't try to be perfect. In your first year, you will plan lessons that don't work, you'll mark tasks too slowly and you'll forget at least one duty. That's normal. What matters is that you reflect, ask for help and improve. The teachers who struggle most are often the ones who hide their problems because they think everyone else is coping.

Second, relationships come before content. Students will not care how much mathematics you know until they know that you care about them. Learn names in the first week, notice when someone is absent and greet your classes at the door. These small things build trust, and trust makes classroom management much easier.

Third, protect your energy. Teaching is a marathon, not a sprint. Set yourself a finishing time each evening and keep at least one day of the weekend free. Use the resources your faculty already has instead of creating everything yourself. And please, eat lunch. I've seen too many new teachers spend every break on the photocopier.

Finally, remember why you chose this profession. On difficult days, think of the student whose face lit up when they finally understood something. Those moments are the reason we do this job. Thank you.

title: Teaching with AI tutors
src:
Artificial intelligence tutoring systems are now being trialled in classrooms around the world. Unlike earlier educational software, which simply marked answers right or wrong, the newest systems can hold a conversation with a student, ask guiding questions and adjust the difficulty of tasks based on each response.

Early studies are promising. In one trial involving secondary mathematics students, those who used an AI tutor for twenty minutes three times a week made noticeably greater progress than a comparison group. Teachers in the trial reported that the system was particularly helpful for students who were reluctant to ask questions in front of their classmates.

However, researchers warn against seeing AI as a replacement for teachers. The systems sometimes give confident but incorrect explanations, and they cannot easily notice when a student is bored, upset or simply guessing. There are also concerns about student data, as many tools are run by private companies.

Most experts recommend a blended approach, in which AI provides extra practice and immediate feedback, while teachers remain responsible for explaining new ideas, building relationships and making decisions about each student's learning.

title: The disappearing keyboard
src:
For many years, it was assumed that young people were 'digital natives' who would naturally become skilled computer users. Recent research suggests this assumption is wrong. Many teenagers are highly confident with smartphones but struggle with basic computer tasks such as typing efficiently, organising files into folders or using a spreadsheet.

One reason is that phones and tablets hide the underlying structure of digital systems. Apps save work automatically, and files are found by searching rather than by understanding where they are stored. As a result, some students are surprised to learn that a document can exist in more than one version or location.

Employers have noticed the gap. In surveys, businesses report that school leavers often lack the practical computer skills needed in office jobs, even when they are comfortable with social media.

In response, some schools have reintroduced keyboarding lessons and explicit teaching of file management in Years 7 and 8. Supporters argue these basic skills free students to focus on higher-level tasks, such as programming and data analysis, later in their schooling.

title: Data and privacy at school
src:
Speaker A: Today I'm joined by Dr Priya Nair, who researches data privacy in schools. Dr Nair, why should parents be concerned?
Speaker B: Well, schools today collect an enormous amount of information: attendance, grades, behaviour notes, medical details and, increasingly, data from learning apps. Speaker A: What kind of harm can that cause?
Speaker B: In the worst cases, identity theft, because children's records are valuable to criminals. Their identities often aren't checked for years, so fraud can go unnoticed for a long time. But there's also a quieter risk: information about a student's behaviour or learning difficulties could follow them in ways that are unfair.
Speaker A: So what should schools be doing?
Speaker B: Three things. First, collect only what they actually need. Second, check carefully where data is stored and who can access it before they adopt a new app. And third, teach students about privacy, so they understand that 'free' apps are often paid for with their data.
Speaker A: And what about teachers?
Speaker B: Teachers play a big role. They should never send student information through personal email or messaging apps, and they should think twice before signing their class up to a new website, however useful it seems.

title: The power of belonging
src:
Students who feel that they belong at school tend to attend more regularly, participate more in class and achieve better results. They are also less likely to experience anxiety and depression. Yet international surveys suggest that around one in four Australian teenagers does not feel a strong sense of belonging at school.

Belonging is shaped by many factors, but relationships with teachers are among the most important. Students who believe that at least one adult at school knows them well and cares about their progress are far more likely to stay engaged, even when they find the work difficult.

Schools are trying different ways to strengthen these connections. Some have introduced small 'home groups' that stay with the same teacher for several years. Others encourage teachers to have brief, positive conversations with every student over the course of a term, and keep a simple record to make sure no one is overlooked.

Co-curricular activities also play a role. Sport, music, robotics teams and debating give students a chance to succeed outside the classroom and to connect with peers who share their interests.

title: Screens before sleep
src:
Most teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night, but studies consistently find that many sleep far less, especially on school nights. Researchers have linked this to the use of phones and other devices late in the evening.

The effect is partly physical. The bright light from screens can delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that helps us fall asleep. But the content matters too. Messaging friends, scrolling through social media or playing online games keeps the brain alert and makes it harder to switch off. Some teenagers also wake during the night to check notifications.

The consequences show up at school. Sleep-deprived students find it harder to concentrate and remember new information, and they are more likely to feel irritable or anxious. Teachers often notice the effects in the first period of the day.

Health experts suggest simple changes, such as charging phones outside the bedroom and stopping screen use an hour before bed. Schools can help by teaching students about sleep and by avoiding homework deadlines late at night.

title: Teaching resilience
src:
Today I want to talk about resilience, which we can define as the ability to adapt and recover when things go wrong. It's a word you'll hear a lot in schools, and sometimes it's misunderstood.

Resilience doesn't mean never feeling upset, and it certainly doesn't mean telling students to 'toughen up'. Resilient people still experience stress and disappointment. The difference is that they have strategies and support that help them recover.

Research suggests three things matter most. The first is relationships. Young people who have at least one caring adult in their lives, whether a parent, a coach or a teacher, cope much better with difficulties. The second is a sense of competence: the belief that effort can lead to improvement. This is where classroom practice really matters. When teachers praise strategies and persistence rather than intelligence, students learn that setbacks are part of learning. The third is practical skills, such as breaking problems into smaller steps, asking for help and managing stress through sleep, exercise and time with friends.

For teachers, the message is encouraging. You don't need to run a special program to build resilience. Every time you help a student try again after a poor test result, or show them how to tackle a difficult problem one step at a time, you are teaching resilience. In mathematics, in particular, students face problems they cannot immediately solve, which makes your classroom an ideal place to practise it.

title: Why students forget
src:
Most teachers have had the frustrating experience of teaching a topic thoroughly, seeing students perform well in a test, and then discovering a few months later that much of the knowledge has disappeared. Cognitive scientists have a name for this: the forgetting curve.

The curve shows that we forget new information rapidly in the days after learning it, unless we revisit it. The good news is that every time information is retrieved from memory, it becomes more durable. This has led researchers to recommend two strategies: spaced practice, in which topics are revisited over weeks and months, and retrieval practice, in which students actively recall information rather than simply re-reading notes.

In mathematics classrooms, these strategies can be built into routines. Many teachers now begin lessons with a short quiz that mixes questions from last week, last month and last term. The questions are low-stakes and not recorded, so students see them as practice rather than assessment.

Students often prefer re-reading because it feels easier and more comfortable. But research consistently shows that the slightly harder work of recalling information leads to much stronger long-term learning.

title: Marking guidelines explained
src:
Every HSC examination is marked using detailed guidelines that describe what a response must contain to earn each mark. In mathematics, for example, a four-mark question may award one mark for setting up the correct equation, one for an appropriate method, one for correct working and one for the final answer with correct units.

Many students are unaware of how these guidelines work. They focus only on the final answer and do not realise that clear working can earn most of the marks even when a calculation error leads to the wrong result. Conversely, a correct answer with no working may receive only one mark.

Teachers increasingly use marking guidelines as a teaching tool rather than only for marking. Students mark sample responses, compare them with the guidelines and discuss why marks were awarded or lost. This helps them understand the standard expected and develop habits such as stating formulas and showing substitution.

The guidelines and sample answers from previous years are freely available online, making them a valuable resource for students preparing independently.

Guidelines are freely available for independent study

title: Preparing for the HSC: advice from a former student
src:
Hi everyone. Two years ago I was sitting exactly where you are, so I want to share what worked for me and what I wish I'd done differently.

The biggest mistake I made in Term 1 was thinking the HSC was a long way off. I did my homework, but I didn't really revise. By Term 3, I had a mountain of topics I'd half forgotten. So my first piece of advice is to review a little every week from now. Even thirty minutes on old topics makes a huge difference.

Second, past papers. I started doing them in August, but I should have started earlier, topic by topic. And don't just check whether you got the right answer. Read the marking guidelines and the markers' comments. That's where I learned how to set out my working so I didn't lose easy marks.

Third, look after your health. In the trial exams, I barely slept, and I did worse than I expected. For the actual HSC, I kept a routine: study in the morning, exercise in the afternoon and no screens after ten. I felt so much calmer.

And finally, ask for help. Teachers really do want to help you, and many of them run extra sessions. I went to the maths revision sessions every Thursday, and that's where things finally clicked for me. Good luck, everyone. You can do this.

title: Parents and maths homework
src:
Many parents want to help their children with mathematics homework but feel unable to do so. Some were taught different methods at school and worry that their explanations will confuse their children. Others had negative experiences with mathematics themselves and fear passing on their anxiety.

Research suggests that how parents help matters more than whether they know the content. When parents take over and show their child how to do a problem, the child may finish the homework but learn little. Similarly, comments such as 'I was never good at maths either' can lower a child's expectations of themselves.

More effective forms of support are surprisingly simple. Parents can provide a regular time and quiet place for homework, ask their child to explain what they are learning and show interest in their progress. Praising effort and persistence, rather than speed or natural ability, also encourages a positive attitude.

Some schools now run short workshops to show parents the methods currently taught in class. These sessions are particularly valuable for families who speak languages other than English at home, as they often include interpreters and visual examples.

title: Schools as community hubs

Supporters argue that this makes good use of expensive public facilities that would otherwise stand empty for much of the year. It can also strengthen relationships between schools and families, particularly in communities where many parents are recent migrants and may feel uncomfortable approaching the school.

One school in Western Sydney, for example, runs English classes for parents on two mornings a week, with free childcare provided. The principal reports that parents who attend are more likely to come to parent–teacher interviews and school events.

There are challenges, however. Opening schools after hours raises questions of security, insurance and cleaning, and someone must manage the bookings. Teachers' unions have also warned that these activities must not add to teachers' already heavy workloads. Successful programs usually employ a dedicated community coordinator and work closely with local councils and organisations.

title: Working with families from diverse backgrounds
src:
Thank you all for coming. In our school, more than seventy percent of students speak a language other than English at home, so building strong partnerships with families is something we have to do deliberately.

I'd like to start with a story. A few years ago, a teacher here was worried because a Year Seven boy never handed in homework. She sent three emails home and got no reply, so she assumed his parents didn't care. When she finally phoned with an interpreter, she discovered that his mother couldn't read English, and his father worked night shifts. They were extremely concerned about their son and very grateful for the call.

The lesson is that silence doesn't mean a lack of interest. Families may face language barriers, unfamiliar school systems or long working hours. Some come from cultures where questioning teachers is considered disrespectful, so they won't contact us even when they are worried.

So what can we do? First, use phone calls and interpreters, not just emails and newsletters. Second, make the first contact positive. Call home to share good news before you ever need to discuss a problem. Third, explain how our system works: things like assessment schedules, reports and subject selection can be confusing for families who were educated overseas.

When families feel welcome and informed, they become our strongest partners in their children's learning.

title: Universal design for learning
src:
Traditionally, teachers planned one lesson for the 'average' student and then made adjustments for students who needed extra support. Universal Design for Learning, or UDL, reverses this approach. It asks teachers to plan lessons that are accessible to as many students as possible from the start.

The idea comes from architecture. Ramps and automatic doors were first designed for people using wheelchairs, but they turned out to benefit everyone, from parents with prams to delivery workers. Similarly, lessons designed with flexibility in mind help a wide range of learners.

In practice, UDL might mean presenting new information in more than one way, for example with a diagram, a worked example and a short video. It might also mean giving students choices in how they show their learning, such as a written explanation, a poster or a recorded presentation.

Critics argue that UDL can be vague and difficult to apply in subjects with fixed content and examinations. Supporters respond that it is a way of thinking rather than a fixed program, and that even small changes, such as providing instructions both verbally and in writing, can make a significant difference.

title: Learning in two languages
src:
About one in four students in Australian schools is learning English as an additional language or dialect. Many of these students are highly capable, but their results may not reflect their ability because of the language demands of the curriculum.

Mathematics is sometimes thought of as a universal language, yet it is full of language challenges. Words such as 'table', 'product' and 'volume' have different meanings in everyday English and in mathematics. Worded problems often contain complex sentences, and students must understand exactly what is being asked before they can begin calculating.

Research shows that students' first language is a valuable resource rather than an obstacle. Students who discuss mathematical ideas in their home language with classmates often develop deeper understanding, which they can then express in English. Bilingual glossaries and visual supports are also effective.

Teachers do not need to speak every language in the classroom. What matters is that they recognise the language demands of their subject and teach the vocabulary and sentence structures that students need, just as they teach mathematical skills.

title: Mathematics behind the scenes
src:
When students ask 'When will I ever use this?', teachers often struggle to give convincing answers. Yet mathematics underpins a surprising range of careers, many of which students never associate with the subject.

In healthcare, nurses calculate medication doses and drip rates, where a decimal error can be dangerous. In construction, builders and electricians use measurement, ratios and trigonometry daily. Chefs scale recipes and manage food costs, while retail managers analyse sales data to decide what to order. Even sports coaches now rely on statistics to plan training and select players.

Technology-related careers depend on mathematics even more heavily. Data analysts, software engineers and cybersecurity specialists use logic, algebra and probability as everyday tools. Australia currently faces shortages in many of these fields.

Career advisers recommend that schools invite people from different industries to explain how they use mathematics. When students hear a nurse, a plumber or a game designer describe their work, mathematics becomes more meaningful, and students are more likely to keep their options open by continuing with the subject.

title: The rise of micro-credentials
src:
For most of the last century, a person's education was largely completed by their early twenties. Today, rapid technological change means that many workers need to update their skills several times during their careers. One response has been the growth of micro-credentials: short courses that certify specific skills, such as data visualisation, cloud computing or project management.

Micro-credentials are attractive because they are flexible and relatively inexpensive. Many can be completed online in a few weeks while working. Some large technology companies offer their own certificates, which are widely recognised by employers.

However, the quality of micro-credentials varies greatly, and employers sometimes find it hard to judge their value. Unlike university degrees, they are not always assessed against agreed national standards. There are also concerns that they focus on narrow technical skills while neglecting broader abilities such as critical thinking and communication.

For schools, the trend reinforces the importance of teaching students how to learn independently. Students who leave school with strong foundations in literacy, numeracy and digital skills are best placed to keep learning throughout their lives.

title: Women in technology
src:
Thank you for inviting me. I'm a software engineer, and I work for a company that builds apps for hospitals. When I was at school, I had no idea this job existed. I liked maths, but I thought computing was something boys did after school playing games.

What changed my mind was a holiday program in Year Ten. For one week, we worked in teams to design an app that helped elderly people remember their medication. I realised that technology could solve real problems for real people, and that it needed creativity and teamwork as much as coding.

Today, women still make up less than a third of the technology workforce in Australia. That's not because girls aren't capable. In fact, girls often do very well in mathematics and computing at school. The problem is that many never imagine themselves in these roles, partly because they don't see people like them doing the work.

So I have two messages tonight. To students: if you enjoy solving problems, technology could be for you, whatever you look like and whatever your background. Try a coding club, enter a competition, or ask about a holiday program. To parents and teachers: encourage girls to keep studying mathematics, even if they're not sure about their future. Mathematics keeps doors open. I nearly closed that door myself, and I'm so glad someone encouraged me to keep it open.

title: Counting the school's energy
src:
When a Western Sydney high school discovered that its annual electricity bill had risen to more than $90,000, the principal turned to an unexpected group for help: the Year 9 mathematics and IPT classes.

Over one term, students installed simple energy monitors in classrooms, collected data every fifteen minutes and analysed the results using spreadsheets. They discovered that air-conditioners in several empty rooms were running all weekend and that computer labs were left on overnight.

The students presented their findings to the school executive with graphs and cost calculations. They recommended timers for air-conditioners, an automatic shutdown setting for lab computers and a 'last out, lights out' campaign. When these changes were introduced, electricity use fell by about eighteen percent in six months, saving the school more than $15,000.

Teachers involved in the project say the benefits went beyond money. Students who rarely engaged in mathematics became enthusiastic when they saw that their calculations led to real decisions. The project also developed skills in data collection, collaboration and presenting to an audience.

title: The problem with e-waste
src:
Every year, Australians generate hundreds of thousands of tonnes of electronic waste, from old phones and laptops to televisions and chargers. E-waste is one of the fastest-growing types of rubbish in the world, and only a small proportion is properly recycled.

This is a problem for two reasons. First, electronic devices contain toxic substances such as lead and mercury, which can leak into soil and water when devices are dumped in landfill. Second, they also contain valuable materials, including gold, copper and rare metals, which are wasted when devices are thrown away.

Schools are significant producers of e-waste, as they regularly replace laptops, projectors and interactive whiteboards. Some schools have responded by extending the life of devices through repairs and upgrades, donating older equipment to community groups and using certified recyclers.

E-waste also offers rich learning opportunities. IPT students can investigate the life cycle of a device, calculate the environmental cost of replacing it and design campaigns encouraging families to recycle old phones responsibly.

title: Teaching sustainability through data
src:
Good morning. I want to show you how sustainability can become one of the most engaging contexts for teaching statistics.

Three years ago, my Year Ten students were bored by textbook data about fictional shoe sizes. So we started using real environmental data instead. The Bureau of Meteorology publishes temperature and rainfall records for every region of Australia, going back more than a hundred years. Students choose a location that matters to them, perhaps where they grew up, or where their grandparents live, and investigate how the climate has changed.

The mathematics is genuine. Students calculate means and medians for different decades, draw box plots, identify outliers and discuss whether changes are significant or just natural variation. Some go further and use spreadsheets to create trend lines.

What surprised me most was the quality of discussion. Students debated how to choose fair comparison periods and whether a few extreme years could distort the results. They were thinking like statisticians.

Of course, there are challenges. Real data is messy. There are missing values and changes in measuring equipment, so students need guidance. Some topics, like climate change, can also cause anxiety, so it's important to focus on investigation and solutions rather than fear.

But overall, I've found that when data is real and personally meaningful, students engage far more deeply than with any textbook example.

title: Lesson study
src:
Lesson study is a form of professional learning that originated in Japan and is now used in schools around the world. Instead of attending a one-off workshop, a small group of teachers works together over several weeks to plan, teach and refine a single lesson.

The process usually begins with the group identifying a problem in students' learning, such as difficulty understanding proportional reasoning. The teachers research the topic and carefully design a lesson to address it. One member then teaches the lesson while the others observe, focusing on how students respond rather than on the teacher's performance.

After the lesson, the group meets to discuss what they observed and revise the plan. Often the lesson is taught again to a different class, and the cycle continues.

Supporters say lesson study builds a culture of collaboration and gives teachers a deeper understanding of how students think. Its main drawback is time: releasing several teachers to plan and observe together is expensive, and some schools find it difficult to sustain. However, many schools report that even one cycle a year can have a lasting effect.

title: Teacher accreditation in NSW
src:
To teach in a NSW school, teachers must be accredited by the NSW Education Standards Authority. New graduates usually begin with conditional or provisional accreditation and must then achieve 'Proficient Teacher' status within a set period.

To do so, they collect evidence showing that their practice meets the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers. These standards cover areas such as knowing students and how they learn, planning effective lessons, creating safe learning environments, assessing learning and engaging with colleagues and families. Evidence might include lesson plans, annotated student work and feedback from observations.

Once accredited at Proficient level, teachers must maintain their accreditation by completing professional development over a five-year cycle. Some choose to apply for higher levels of accreditation, which recognise highly accomplished and lead teachers.

For teachers whose first language is not English, there is an additional requirement before accreditation: evidence of English language proficiency, such as an ISLPR result of at least Level 4 in each of speaking, listening, reading and writing.

title: Reflective practice
src:
Today's topic is reflective practice, which simply means thinking carefully about your own teaching in order to improve it. Every experienced teacher you admire does this, often without even noticing.

Reflection isn't the same as worrying. Lying awake replaying a lesson that went badly is not reflection. Reflection is structured. It asks specific questions: What did I want students to learn? What evidence do I have that they learned it? What will I do differently next time?

The key word there is evidence. Too often, we judge a lesson by how it felt. A lively, noisy lesson might feel successful, but did students actually learn the content? On the other hand, a quiet lesson might feel flat, yet students may have made real progress. Exit tickets, student work and short quizzes give you evidence beyond your feelings.

There are many ways to make reflection a habit. Some teachers keep a brief journal, writing three sentences after each lesson. Others record a lesson occasionally and watch it back, which can be uncomfortable but very revealing. Many find it most useful to reflect with a colleague, because another person notices things we miss.

During your placements, you've been required to write reflections. I encourage you not to see them as paperwork, but as the beginning of a professional habit that will make you a better teacher throughout your career.

title: Teaching students to spot fake news
src:
Young people now get much of their news from social media, where accurate reporting, opinion, advertising and deliberate misinformation appear side by side. Surveys suggest that many teenagers find it difficult to tell the difference, and some trust information simply because it has been shared many times.

Teachers across all subjects can help students become more critical consumers of information. In mathematics, for example, students can analyse misleading graphs: axes that do not start at zero, cherry-picked time periods or percentages without the original numbers. Seeing how statistics can be manipulated helps students question claims they encounter online.

In IPT, students can learn how algorithms decide what appears in their feeds, and why content that provokes strong emotions tends to spread faster. Understanding these systems makes students less likely to be manipulated.

Researchers recommend teaching simple habits, such as checking who created a piece of content, looking for the same story on reliable news sites and pausing before sharing anything that causes a strong emotional reaction.

title: Passwords and the human factor
src:
Many people imagine cybersecurity breaches as the work of brilliant hackers breaking through complex defences. In reality, a large proportion of attacks succeed because of simple human errors: weak or reused passwords, clicking on links in fake emails, or sharing information with someone pretending to be from IT support.

Schools are attractive targets because they hold personal information about thousands of students and families, yet often have limited security budgets. In recent years, several schools have had systems locked by ransomware, disrupting classes and reports for weeks.

Experts recommend several practical steps. Staff and students should use long passphrases rather than short passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication, which requires a second code in addition to a password. Regular training helps people recognise phishing emails, which often create a sense of urgency, such as 'Your account will be closed today.'

IPT teachers are well placed to teach these skills, but cybersecurity is everyone's responsibility. A single click by one staff member can affect the entire school.

title: Teenagers and social media
src:
Speaker A: With me is Professor Tom Walsh, who studies young people and technology. Professor, is social media harming teenagers?
Speaker B: It's more complicated than a simple yes or no. For many young people, social media is where they maintain friendships, find communities and explore interests. For teenagers from minority groups or rural areas, these connections can be really valuable.
Speaker A: But there are concerns about mental health.
Speaker B: Yes, and they're real. Heavy use, especially late at night, is linked to poorer sleep, and poor sleep affects mood. Some platforms are designed to keep users scrolling, and constant comparison with carefully edited images can affect self-esteem, particularly among girls.
Speaker A: Some governments are introducing age limits. Do you support that?
Speaker B: I understand the motivation, but age limits are difficult to enforce. Many children simply lie about their age. I think the bigger priorities are safer design, such as limits on endless scrolling, and education, so that young people understand how platforms work.
Speaker A: What can schools do?
Speaker B: Schools can teach digital literacy across subjects, involve parents and, importantly, listen to students. Young people often have very good ideas about what would make their online lives healthier, but they're rarely asked.
